# ==========================================
# File: core/app-patterns.mdx
# ==========================================

# App Organization Patterns

Cequre gives you two ways to organize application code — custom routes, hooks, access rules, and crons — around the app instance. Both are first-class; they answer different questions. This page explains what each is for and when to reach for it.

## Pattern 1: The Exported App (composition root)

The app itself is a **value** you create once and export. Everything else in your project imports it and registers directly on it.

```typescript
// cequre/app.ts — pure construction. No routes, no boot.
import { createCequre } from "./_generated/server";
import { PostgresAdapter, defaultSecurity } from "cequre-ts";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new PostgresAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
  plugins: [defaultSecurity()],
});

export type APP = typeof app;
```

```typescript
// cequre/routes.ts — imports the app, registers directly on it
import { app } from "./app";

app.get("/health", () => ({ status: "ok" }));

app.get("/previews/:id", async (ctx) => {
  return Response.json(await getPreview(ctx.params.id));
});
```

```typescript
// cequre/index.ts — just boots
import "./routes";              // side-effect import: this IS the wiring
import { app } from "./app";

app.start({ port: Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000 });
```

### Why it works without generics

Notice there is no `<Collections>` anywhere. The typing comes from **construction**, not declaration: `createCequre` in `_generated/server.ts` already pins its generic to your compiled schema, so every route registered on the exported `app` inherits fully typed `ctx` (including typed `ctx.user`) with zero type annotations.

The rule of thumb: **type where you create, not where you use.**

### What the exported app unlocks

Because `app` is a plain exported value, it composes beyond the server process:

| Consumer | How |
|---|---|
| Server entry (`index.ts`) | `app.start({ port })` |
| Serverless / edge hosts | `export const handleRequest = (req: Request) => app.fetch(req)` |
| Tests (no port binding) | `const res = await app.fetch(new Request("http://x/api/..."))` |
| Sub-routers / internal calls | Any module imports `{ app }` and registers or fetches |

## Pattern 2: `CequreModule` (distributable units)

A `CequreModule` is a **deferred registration bundle**: it collects routes, access rules, hooks, and crons into a value that can be applied later to an app via `.use()`.

```typescript
// cequre/routes.ts
import { CequreModule, t } from "cequre-ts";
import type { Collections } from "./_generated/server";

export const routesModule = new CequreModule<Collections>();

routesModule.get("/greeting", () => ({ greeting: "hello from cequre" }), {
  response: t.Object({ greeting: t.String() }),
});

routesModule.hooks("todos", {
  beforeCreate: async (ctx) => {
    if (!ctx.data.author) ctx.data.author = ctx.user?.id || "anonymous";
    return ctx.data;
  },
});
```

```typescript
// cequre/index.ts — applied at the composition root
export const app = createCequre({ adapter, plugins })
  .use(routesModule);
```

Nothing runs at module definition time — registrations are buffered in `_setupFns` and only execute when `.use()` applies them to an app.

### What `CequreModule` is actually for

Its defining property is **decoupling from any specific app instance**. That makes it the right tool exactly when code must outlive one project:

1. **Distributable packages** — a published npm package of routes/hooks/access rules that other Cequre apps install and `.use()` with their own adapter and config.
2. **Multi-app reuse** — the same admin module mounted in both a staging app and a production app.
3. **Feature isolation in large teams** — team A ships `billingModule`, team B ships `analyticsModule`; neither touches the composition root, and each is testable in isolation against a mock app.

If your code will never leave the app it lives in, a module adds indirection without adding value — use Pattern 1.

Note the one place modules cost more typing: because a module is declared *away* from the app's construction site, it cannot infer `Collections` — you import the type explicitly (`new CequreModule<Collections>()`). That is the trade-off for portability.

## Choosing Between Them

| | Exported App | `CequreModule` |
|---|---|---|
| Typing | Inferred from construction — no annotations | Requires explicit `<Collections>` |
| Wiring | File list (`import "./routes"`) is the wiring | Explicit `.use()` per module |
| Lifecycle | Registrations run immediately | Deferred until `.use()` |
| Reusable across apps | No — bound to one app | Yes — the whole point |
| Publishable as a package | Awkward | Natural |
| Best for | App-scoped features (the default) | Distributable/feature-packaged code |

A common hybrid in bigger projects: the app's own features use Pattern 1, while genuinely reusable pieces (auth flows, billing, tenant tooling) are extracted into modules and `.use()`d like third-party plugins.

## Related

- [Custom Endpoints](../ts/custom-endpoints) — Route handlers, context, schema validation
- [Project Structure](./project-structure) — Where these files live in the scaffold


# ==========================================
# File: core/basic-usage.mdx
# ==========================================

# Basic Usage

The fastest way to start building with Cequre is using our official project initializer. It sets up a new Cequre project with a recommended directory structure, a default configuration, and everything you need to start building immediately.

## 1. Initialize a New Project

Once you have installed the Cequre binary, you can initialize a new project anywhere on your system:

```bash
cequre init
```

During initialization, the CLI will guide you through a few quick questions:
- **What is your project named?** (e.g., `my-cequre-app`)
- **Choose a template** (Blank, Auth, E-commerce, etc.)
- **Where should the generated gen.ts be outputted?** (e.g., `.`)

Once the setup is complete, navigate into your new project directory:

```bash
cd my-cequre-app
```

## 2. Define Your First Collection

Open `cequre/collections.cequre` in your code editor. Let's add a simple `posts` collection to see how easy it is to model data:

```cequre
collection posts {
  fields: {
    title: text
    content: text
    published: boolean @default(false)
  }
}
```

This simple definition is enough for Cequre to generate a full CRUD API, TypeScript interfaces, and database schema!

## 3. Start the Development Server

To see your new API in action, start the Cequre development server:

```bash
cequre dev
```

This command does a lot of heavy lifting for you automatically:
1. **Compiles** your `.cequre` files into an optimized runtime schema.
2. **Generates** TypeScript definitions (`cequre-types.ts`) for your frontend or custom hooks.
3. **Starts** the built-in API server on `http://localhost:3000`.

## 4. Test Your API

With the server running, Cequre has automatically created all the standard REST endpoints for your `posts` collection.

You can instantly test creating a new post:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title": "My First Cequre Post", "content": "This backend was built in seconds."}'
```

And fetch it back:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts
```

## What's Next?

You have a fully functional API running! From here, you can:
- Define more complex [Collections](./collections) and relationships.
- Add custom [Access Control](./access) rules to secure your endpoints.
- Check out the auto-generated Swagger UI at `http://localhost:3000/api/docs`.


# ==========================================
# File: core/bun-adapter.mdx
# ==========================================

# The Bun Runtime

Bun is the runtime for Cequre. It natively supports Web Standards (Fetch, WebSockets, Web Streams), making the runtime incredibly lightweight and blazingly fast.

### Installation

If you generated your project using `cequre init`, Bun is already configured and the runtime is embedded — no separate package install is needed. The CLI extracts the runtime (including all database drivers: `postgres`, `mongodb`, `surrealdb`, `@libsql/client`) into `cequre/_generated/runtime/` and aliases `cequre-ts` to it in `tsconfig.json`. You import everything from the bare `cequre-ts` specifier:

```ts
import { defaultSecurity } from "cequre-ts";
```

### Usage

Pass your configuration directly to `createCequre`. The Bun server, cron scheduler, WebSocket provider, and local storage are wired in automatically — no wrapper required.

```ts
import { createCequre } from "../_generated/server";
import { defaultSecurity } from "cequre-ts";

// 1. Define your configuration
const config = {
  plugins: [defaultSecurity()]
};

// 2. Create the app
const app = createCequre(config);

// 3. Start the server
await app.start({ port: 3000 });
```

### Starting the Server

Simply run your file using the `bun` CLI:

```bash
bun run cequre/index.ts
```

# ==========================================
# File: core/cli-reference.mdx
# ==========================================

# CLI Reference

The Cequre CLI (`cequre`) provides commands for project initialization, code generation, development, database sync, and language server support.

## Installation

The Cequre CLI is a **single Go-built standalone binary**. There is no `@cequrebackends/cequre` npm package — the CLI ships as a compiled executable, and scaffolded projects invoke the same `cequre` binary on your `PATH`.

## Commands

### `cequre init`

Initialize a new Cequre project in the current directory.

```bash
cequre init
cequre init --dir my-app
```

**Options:**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-d, --dir <path>` | Project directory name | Interactive prompt |

**What it does:**

1. Prompts for a project name (if not provided via `--dir`)
2. Prompts for a template (currently: `blank`)
3. Creates a `<project>/cequre/schema/` directory
4. Writes the template's `config.cequre` boilerplate into `cequre/schema/`
5. Scaffolds `cequre/index.ts` (composition root) and `cequre/routes.ts` (custom routes module)
6. Writes `.env` with `JWT_SECRET` and `DATABASE_URL`
7. Prints next steps

The blank template creates a starter `config.cequre` with basic security and monitoring settings, plus a `users` collection with auth enabled.

### `cequre generate`

Compile `.cequre` files and generate runtime artifacts.

```bash
cequre generate
cequre generate --runtime ts --dir ./cequre
cequre generate --runtime go --dir ./cequre
```

**Options:**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-r, --runtime <type>` | Target runtime (`ts` for TypeScript/Bun, `go` for Go) | `ts` |
| `-d, --dir <path>` | Path to the `cequre/` directory | `./cequre` |

**What it does:**

1. Finds all `.cequre` files in the `cequre/` directory (recursively)
2. Lexes and parses each file
3. Compiles all ASTs into a unified schema (with semantic validation)
4. Generates output files:
   - `node_modules/.cequre/schema.json` — compiled schema
   - `cequre/_generated/runtime/` — embedded runtime bundle (TS target)
   - `cequre/_generated/server.ts` — runtime SDK entry point (TS target)
   - `cequre/_generated/client.ts` — client SDK (TS target)
   - `cequre/_generated/schemas.ts` — TypeBox schemas (TS target)
   - `cequre/_generated/*.go` — standalone Go module (Go target: `main.go`, `models.go`, `store.go`, `populate.go`, `router.go`, `auth.go`, `go.mod`)

For the **Go target**, the CLI writes the full Go module and verifies it with `go mod tidy` + `go build`. Build and run it with:

```bash
cd cequre/_generated
go build -o cequre-app .
./cequre-app
```

See [Go Runtime](./runtime) for the generated API surface.

If any lexing, parsing, or semantic errors occur, the command prints them and exits with code 1 (unless in dev mode).

### `cequre dev`

Watch `.cequre` files and rebuild on changes.

```bash
cequre dev
cequre dev --runtime ts
```

**Options:**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-r, --runtime <type>` | Target runtime | `ts` |
| `-d, --dir <path>` | Path to the `cequre/` directory | `./cequre` |

**What it does:**

1. Runs an initial `generateCompilerOutput` (same as `cequre generate`)
2. Watches the `cequre/` directory with chokidar (ignoring generated outputs)
3. On any `.cequre` file change, debounces for 100ms, then recompiles
4. In dev mode, compilation errors are printed but the process does not exit — you fix and save again

This is the primary development workflow: run `cequre dev` in one terminal and `bun run --hot cequre/index.ts` in another.

### `cequre db:sync`

Sync the database schema against the compiled `.cequre` schema.

```bash
cequre db:sync
cequre db:sync --force
cequre db:sync --dir ./cequre
```

**Options:**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-d, --dir <path>` | Path to the `cequre/` directory | `./cequre` |
| `--force` | Apply destructive changes (drop orphaned tables/columns) | `false` |

**What it does:**

1. Loads the compiled `node_modules/.cequre/schema.json`
2. Reads `DATABASE_URL` from the environment (or `.env` file)
3. Creates a database adapter based on the URL scheme:
   - `file:` / `sqlite:` → SQLite adapter
   - `postgres:` / `postgresql:` → PostgreSQL adapter
   - `redis:` → Redis adapter
   - `http:` / `https:` → SurrealDB adapter
4. Computes a schema diff:
   - **Tables to create** — collections that don't exist in the database
   - **Columns to add** — fields that don't exist in existing tables
   - **Tables to drop** — database tables not in the schema (orphaned)
   - **Columns to drop** — database columns not in the schema (orphaned)
5. Prints the diff report
6. Applies non-destructive changes (create tables, add columns)
7. Applies destructive changes only if `--force` is provided
8. In production (`NODE_ENV=production`), destructive changes are always skipped unless `--force`

**Example output:**

```
📡 Connecting to database...
📊 Comparing schema against database...

  + Tables to create:
      + todos
  + Columns to add:
      + users.role
  - Columns to drop:
      - users.legacyField

  ⚠ Skipping destructive changes (no --force flag).

⚙️  Applying changes...
  + Creating table: todos
  + Adding column: users.role

✅ Schema sync complete.
```

### `cequre lsp`

Run the Cequre Language Server (for editor integration).

```bash
cequre lsp
```

This starts the LSP server on stdio. It's used by the VS Code extension. You typically don't run this manually — the editor launches it.

See [Editor Support](./editor-support) for details.

### `cequre add <item>`

Add an integration plugin or framework adapter to an existing project. This is a shorthand that works for both plugins (`s3`, `resend`, `nodemailer`, `durable-streams`) and adapters (`vite`).

```bash
# Add a plugin
cequre add s3
cequre add resend

# Add an adapter — interactive (prompts for target, database, output path)
cequre add vite

# Add an adapter — non-interactive with flags
cequre add vite -t bun -d turso -o cequre --plugins security,monitoring
```

**Options:**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-t, --target <target>` | Deployment target: `bun` or `node` | Prompted interactively |
| `-d, --db <adapter>` | Database adapter: `sqlite`, `postgres`, `surrealdb`, `turso`, or `mongodb` | Prompted interactively |
| `-u, --url <url>` | Database connection URL | Prompted interactively (or derived from adapter) |
| `-o, --output <path>` | Output directory for server files (relative to root) | Prompted interactively |
| `--plugins <plugins>` | Comma-separated built-in plugins: `security,monitoring,adminUi` | Prompted interactively |

### `cequre plugin add <name>`

Scaffold an integration plugin into your project. Creates `cequre/plugins/<name>/index.ts`, updates the barrel file at `cequre/plugins/index.ts`, and appends required env vars to `.env`.

```bash
cequre plugin add s3
cequre plugin add resend
cequre plugin add nodemailer
cequre plugin add durable-streams
```

**Available plugins:**

| Plugin | Category | Package |
|---|---|---|
| `s3` | Storage | `aws4fetch` |
| `resend` | Email | `resend` |
| `nodemailer` | Email | `nodemailer` |
| `durable-streams` | Streams | `ioredis` |

**What it does:**

1. Creates `cequre/plugins/<name>/index.ts` with a fully typed scaffold implementing a Cequre interface
2. Appends `export * from "./<name>";` to `cequre/plugins/index.ts` barrel file
3. Appends required env vars to `.env` (or `.env.local`) with a comment header
4. Installs the npm package(s) via your detected package manager

See [Plugins](./plugins) for details on each scaffolded plugin and how to wire them in.

### `cequre adapter add <name>`

Add a framework or frontend adapter to your project. Currently supports `vite`.

```bash
cequre adapter add vite
```

**What it does (Vite):**

1. Detects `vite.config.ts` (or `.js` / `.mjs`) in the current directory
2. Injects `cequreVite({ autoBuild: true })` into Vite's plugin array
3. Adds `@cequrebackends/plugin-vite` to `package.json` dependencies
4. Scaffolds `cequre/schema/config.cequre` if not already present

See [Vite Integration](./vite-plugin) for full details.

### `cequre client <url>`

Download the generated TypeScript client SDK from a running Cequre backend server.

```bash
cequre client http://localhost:3000
cequre client http://localhost:3000 -o src/cequre-sdk.ts
cequre client http://localhost:3000 --output src/sdk.ts
```

**Options:**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-o, --output <path>` | Output filepath for the client SDK | `cequre-client.ts` |

### `cequre format`

Format all `.cequre` DSL files in the project directory using Cequre's built-in AST formatter.

```bash
cequre format
cequre format --dir ./cequre
```

**Options:**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-d, --dir <path>` | Path to the `cequre/` directory | `./cequre` |

### `cequre upgrade`

Check GitHub Releases for the latest Cequre CLI binary and automatically perform an in-place executable upgrade.

```bash
cequre upgrade
```

## Project Lifecycle

Here's the typical workflow:

```bash
# 1. Initialize a new project
cequre init --dir my-app
cd my-app

# 2. Edit your schema
# Edit cequre/schema/config.cequre, add collection files, etc.

# 3. Start the dev watcher (recompiles on save)
cequre dev

# 4. In another terminal, start the server
bun run --hot cequre/index.ts

# 5. After schema changes, sync the database
cequre db:sync

# 6. For production builds
cequre generate
bun build cequre/index.ts --outdir dist --target bun
```

## Exit Codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Success |
| `1` | Compilation error (lexing, parsing, or semantic) or missing prerequisites |

# ==========================================
# File: core/collections.mdx
# ==========================================

# Collections

A `collection` block defines a data model — a database table (in SQL databases) or a document collection (in document databases). Each collection automatically gets CRUD API endpoints.

## Syntax

```cequre
collection <name> {
  auth: true
  fields: {
    // field definitions
  }
  realtime: { ... }
  cache: { ... }
  hooks: { ... }
  admin: { ... }
}
```

The collection name must be a valid identifier (`[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*`) and must be unique across all `.cequre` files.

## Allowed Properties

| Property | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `auth` | Boolean | Marks this collection as the authentication collection. Only one collection should have `auth: true`. |
| `emails` | Object | Automated email settings for this collection (`verify_email`, `resend_if_expire`). |
| `fields` | Object | The field definitions for this collection. See [Field Types](./field-types). |
| `realtime` | Object | Realtime subscription settings (WebSocket, SSE, durable streams). |
| `cache` | Object | Caching settings (TTL, strategy). |
| `hooks` | Object | Lifecycle hook references. |
| `admin` | Object | Admin UI settings for this collection. |

## `auth`

When `auth: true`, the collection is treated as the user collection. The runtime enables login, registration, password reset, and token refresh endpoints for it. The runtime also hashes the `password` field automatically.

```cequre
collection users {
  auth: true
  emails: {
    verify_email: true
    resend_if_expire: true
  }
  fields: {
    name: text
    email: email @unique
    password: password
    role: text @default("user")
  }
}
```

### Email Verification (`emails`)

When `emails: { verify_email: true }` is enabled on an auth collection:
- Registration (`POST /api/<slug>/register`) suppresses issuing JWT session tokens and requires the user to verify their email first.
- Login (`POST /api/<slug>/login`) blocks unverified accounts with `403 Forbidden`.
- Setting `resend_if_expire: true` automatically generates and emails a fresh verification link if an unverified user attempts to log in or clicks an expired link (enforcing a 60-second cooldown per user).
- A manual resend endpoint (`POST /api/<slug>/resend-verification`) is exposed for users to request fresh verification links.

The CLI injects two server-managed fields into the collection when verification is enabled: `_verified` (boolean, default `false`) and `_verificationToken` (text, optional). Both are injected with `hidden` + `omit`, meaning they are **never accepted from client payloads** (register, create, or update) and **never returned in API responses** — a client cannot spoof `_verified: true` to bypass verification, and the flags are only visible through server-side code. The same `hidden` + `omit` treatment applies to the MFA fields (`mfaEnabled`, `mfaSecret`, `mfaBackupCodes`) injected when `security.auth.mfa.enabled` is set.

## `fields`

The `fields` block contains field definitions as key-value pairs. Each key is the field name, and the value is the field type (an identifier or function call):

```cequre
collection todos {
  fields: {
    title: text
    completed: boolean @default(false)
    priority: select("low", "medium", "high")
    author: relationship("users")
    tags: text[]
    metadata: json @optional
  }
}
```

Every collection automatically gets an `id` field (UUID string), plus `createdAt` and `updatedAt` timestamp fields managed by the runtime.

See the [Field Types](./field-types) page for all available types and the [Decorators](./decorators) page for `@unique`, `@optional`, `@default`, etc.

## `realtime`

Realtime subscriptions push change events to connected clients in real time.

```cequre
collection todos {
  realtime: {
    ws: ["create", "update", "delete"]
    sse: true
    durableStream: false
  }
  fields: {
    // ...
  }
}
```

| Property | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ws` | String[] | Events to broadcast over WebSocket: `"create"`, `"update"`, `"delete"`. |
| `sse` | Boolean | Enable Server-Sent Events for this collection. |
| `durableStream` | Boolean | Enable a durable stream (persisted event log) for replay. |

## `cache`

Per-collection caching with configurable TTL and strategy:

```cequre
collection products {
  cache: {
    ttl: 3600
    strategy: "stale-while-revalidate"
  }
  fields: {
    // ...
  }
}
```

| Property | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ttl` | Number | Time-to-live in seconds. |
| `strategy` | String | Cache strategy: `"stale-while-revalidate"`, `"cache-first"`, `"network-first"`. |

## `hooks`

Lifecycle hooks run before or after CRUD operations. Hook handlers are written in TypeScript in `cequre/routes.ts` (not in the DSL). The `hooks` property in the DSL is a reference/flag that the runtime uses to register them:

```cequre
collection todos {
  hooks: {
    beforeCreate: true
    afterCreate: true
    beforeUpdate: true
  }
  fields: {
    // ...
  }
}
```

The actual hook logic is defined in TypeScript:

```typescript
// cequre/routes.ts
routesModule.hooks("todos", {
  beforeCreate: async (ctx) => {
    if (!ctx.data.author) ctx.data.author = ctx.user?.id || "anonymous";
    return ctx.data;
  },
  afterCreate: async (ctx) => {
    console.log("Todo created:", ctx.data.id);
  },
});
```

## `admin`

Admin UI settings for this collection:

```cequre
collection products {
  admin: {
    list: ["name", "price", "status"]
    searchable: true
    pageSize: 25
  }
  fields: {
    // ...
  }
}
```

## Auto-Generated API Routes

Every collection gets these REST endpoints (mounted under the API prefix):

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/<slug>` | List records with filtering, pagination, and sorting. |
| `POST` | `/<slug>` | Create a new record. |
| `GET` | `/<slug>/:id` | Get a single record by ID. |
| `PUT` | `/<slug>/:id` | Update a record by ID. |
| `DELETE` | `/<slug>/:id` | Delete a record by ID. |

For a collection named `todos` with API prefix `/api`:

```
GET    /api/todos
POST   /api/todos
GET    /api/todos/:id
PUT    /api/todos/:id
DELETE /api/todos/:id
```

## Cross-File References

Collections can reference each other across files. The compiler merges all `.cequre` files and validates relationship targets:

```cequre
// cequre/users.cequre
collection users {
  auth: true
  fields: {
    name: text
    email: email @unique
  }
}
```

```cequre
// cequre/posts.cequre
collection posts {
  fields: {
    title: text
    author: relationship("users")  // references the users collection
  }
}
```

If `relationship("users")` targets a collection that doesn't exist, the compiler produces a semantic error.

# ==========================================
# File: core/config-block.mdx
# ==========================================

# The Config Block

The `config {}` block defines framework-wide settings: API configuration, security policies, monitoring, admin UI, database migration behaviour, and output directory. It appears once across all `.cequre` files.

## Syntax

```cequre
config {
  // Top-level keys (each is optional):
  core: { ... }
  security: { ... }
  monitoring: { ... }
  adminUi: { ... }
  apiPrefix: "..."
  migrate: { ... }
  output: "..."
}
```

## Allowed Keys

Only these top-level keys are valid inside `config {}`. Unknown keys produce a compile-time error:

| Key          | Type   | Description                                                   |
| ------------ | ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `core`       | Object | Core framework settings (API, OpenAPI, uploads).              |
| `security`   | Object | Authentication, CORS, rate limiting, headers, secrets, audit. |
| `monitoring` | Object | Health checks, request ID tracking.                           |
| `adminUi`    | Object | Admin dashboard configuration.                                |
| `apiPrefix`  | String | Shorthand for `core.api.prefix`.                              |
| `migrate`    | Object | Database migration behaviour.                                 |
| `output`     | String | Output directory for generated files (relative to `cequre/`). |

## `core`

Core framework settings. Allowed keys: `api`, `openapi`, `graphql`, `upload`.

### `api`

```cequre
config {
  core: {
    api: {
      prefix: "/api"          // API route prefix
      maxBodyBytes: 1048576   // Max request body size in bytes
      trustedProxies: ["127.0.0.1"]  // Trusted proxy IPs
    }
  }
}
```

| Property         | Type     | Default         | Description                                            |
| ---------------- | -------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `prefix`         | String   | `"/api"`        | Prefix for all generated API routes.                   |
| `maxBodyBytes`   | Number   | `1048576` (1MB) | Maximum request body size.                             |
| `trustedProxies` | String[] | `[]`            | IP addresses of trusted proxies for header forwarding. |

### `openapi`

```cequre
config {
  core: {
    openapi: {
      enabled: true
      path: "/api/docs"
    }
  }
}
```

When enabled, the runtime serves an OpenAPI/Swagger specification at the configured path.

### `graphql`

```cequre
config {
  core: {
    graphql: {
      enabled: true
      path: "/graphql"
      playground: true
      introspection: true
    }
  }
}
```

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `Boolean` | `false` | Enable the native GraphQL engine and HTTP handler. |
| `path` | `String` | `"/graphql"` | Mount path for the GraphQL endpoint. |
| `playground` | `Boolean` | `true` (dev) | Serves the interactive GraphiQL / Altair explorer for browser requests. |
| `introspection` | `Boolean` | `true` (dev) | Allows schema introspection queries. |

See the [GraphQL Guide](../ts/graphql) for complete query syntax, mutation examples, and relationship querying.

### `upload`

```cequre
config {
  core: {
    upload: {
      maxFileSize: 10485760  // 10MB
      allowedTypes: ["image/png", "image/jpeg"]
    }
  }
}
```

## `security`

Security policies. Allowed keys: `auth`, `cors`, `rateLimit`, `headers`, `secrets`, `audit`, `csrfTrustedOrigins`.

### `auth`

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    auth: {
      strategies: ["jwt", "session"]
      jwt: {
        accessTokenExpiry: env("JWT_EXPIRY", "15m")
        refreshTokenExpiry: "7d"
        cookies: {
          name: "cequre_auth"
          timeout: "7d"
          refreshToken: true
          secure: true
          httpOnly: true
          sameSite: "lax"
          domain: "example.com"
        }
      }
      passwordPolicy: {
        minLength: 8
        requireUppercase: true
        requireNumber: true
      }
      lockout: {
        maxAttempts: env("LOGIN_ATTEMPTS", 5)
        durationMinutes: 15
      }
    }
  }
}
```

| Sub-property           | Type     | Description                                                                        |
| ---------------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `strategies`           | String[] | Auth strategies to enable: `"jwt"`, `"session"`, `"apiKey"`.                       |
| `jwt`                  | Object   | JWT settings: `accessTokenExpiry`, `refreshTokenExpiry`, `cookies`.                |
| `cookies`              | Object   | JWT Cookie configuration properties.                                               |
| `cookies.name`         | String   | Base name for the cookie. Default: `"cequre_auth"`.                                |
| `cookies.timeout`      | String   | Time before the cookie expires (e.g. `"7d"`).                                      |
| `cookies.refreshToken` | Boolean  | Enable a separate cookie for the refresh token. Default: `false`.                  |
| `cookies.secure`       | Boolean  | Emit `Secure` flag for HTTPS only. Default: `false`.                               |
| `cookies.httpOnly`     | Boolean  | Emit `HttpOnly` flag. Default: `false`.                                            |
| `cookies.sameSite`     | String   | SameSite policy (`"lax"`, `"strict"`, `"none"`). Default: `"lax"`.                 |
| `cookies.domain`       | String   | Specifies the allowed domain for the cookie.                                       |
| `session`              | Object   | Session-based auth settings.                                                       |
| `apiKey`               | Object   | API key auth settings: `header` (header name, defaults to `X-API-Key`), `enabled`. |
| `passwordPolicy`       | Object   | `minLength`, `requireUppercase`, `requireNumber`.                                  |
| `lockout`              | Object   | `maxAttempts`, `durationMinutes` — lock accounts after repeated failures.          |

### `cors`

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    cors: {
      origin: ["http://localhost:3000", "https://myapp.com"]
      credentials: true
    }
  }
}
```

| Property      | Type     | Description                                                    |
| ------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `origin`      | String[] | Allowed origin URLs.                                           |
| `credentials` | Boolean  | Whether to allow credentials (cookies, Authorization headers). |

### `rateLimit`

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    rateLimit: {
      write: {
        max: 100
        window: "15m"
      }
      login: {
        max: 5
        window: "15m"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

| Property | Type   | Description                                                                       |
| -------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `write`  | Object | Rate limit for write operations (POST, PUT, DELETE). `max` requests per `window`. |
| `login`  | Object | Rate limit for login attempts. `max` attempts per `window`.                       |
| `max`    | Number | Maximum number of requests in the window.                                         |
| `window` | String | Time window (e.g., `"15m"`, `"1h"`, `"30s"`).                                     |

### `headers`

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    headers: {
      enabled: true
    }
  }
}
```

When enabled, the runtime adds the following security headers to every response:

| Header                      | Value                                      |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `X-Content-Type-Options`    | `nosniff`                                  |
| `X-Frame-Options`           | `DENY`                                     |
| `X-XSS-Protection`          | `1; mode=block`                            |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`      |
| `Referrer-Policy`           | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`          |
| `Permissions-Policy`        | `geolocation=(), microphone=(), camera=()` |

### `secrets`

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    secrets: {
      enabled: true
    }
  }
}
```

When enabled, the runtime provides a secret management API for storing and retrieving encrypted values.

### `audit`

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    audit: {
      enabled: true
    }
  }
}
```

When enabled, the runtime auto-creates a `cequre_audit_log` collection and logs all data mutations with HMAC-signed entries for tamper detection.

### `csrfTrustedOrigins`

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    csrfTrustedOrigins: ["https://myapp.com", "https://admin.myapp.com"]
  }
}
```

| Property             | Type     | Description                                                                                              |
| -------------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `csrfTrustedOrigins` | String[] | Origins allowed to make cookie-authenticated state-changing requests, bypassing same-origin CSRF checks. |

The runtime's CSRF guard activates on state-changing methods (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) when a cookie is present. It checks the `Origin` or `Referer` header against the request `Host`. If the origin doesn't match, the request is rejected with `403 CSRF_ERROR` — unless the origin is listed in `csrfTrustedOrigins`. Requests carrying a custom header (`X-CEQURE-CSRF`, `X-CSRF-Token`, or `X-Requested-With`) bypass the origin check entirely, as custom headers cannot be sent cross-origin without CORS permission.

## `monitoring`

```cequre
config {
  monitoring: {
    enabled: true
    apiKey: env("MONITORING_API_KEY")
    healthCheck: {
      enabled: true
      path: "/health"
      requiresAuth: false
    }
    requestId: {
      enabled: true
    }
  }
}
```

| Property                   | Type    | Description                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`                  | Boolean | Enable monitoring endpoints and request instrumentation.                                                      |
| `apiKey`                   | String  | Bearer token required to access monitoring endpoints. If unset, endpoints are insecure (a warning is logged). |
| `healthCheck.enabled`      | Boolean | Enable the health check endpoint. Defaults to `true` when monitoring is enabled.                              |
| `healthCheck.path`         | String  | URL path for the health check (e.g., `"/health"`). Defaults to `/{apiPrefix}/monitor/health`.                 |
| `healthCheck.requiresAuth` | Boolean | Whether the health check requires the monitoring API key. Defaults to `false`.                                |
| `requestId.enabled`        | Boolean | Generate a unique request ID for each request (honours incoming `X-Request-ID` header).                       |

When monitoring is enabled, the runtime exposes four endpoints under `{apiPrefix}/monitor`:

| Endpoint           | Method | Description                                                                                                     |
| ------------------ | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/monitor/events`  | GET    | Query buffered monitoring events with filters (`?type=`, `?severity=`, `?since=`, `?limit=`).                   |
| `/monitor/metrics` | GET    | Aggregate summary: event counts by type/severity, request totals, average duration.                             |
| `/monitor/health`  | GET    | Database + cache health check. Returns `200` (ok/degraded) or `503` (error).                                    |
| `/monitor/stream`  | GET    | Server-Sent Events live stream with backlog replay and 30s heartbeat. Supports same query filters as `/events`. |

See [Monitoring](./monitoring) for the full guide on exporters, SSE streams, and external tool integration.

## `adminUi`

```cequre
config {
  adminUi: {
    collection: "admins"
    title: "My App Admin"
    logo: "/logo.svg"
  }
}
```

| Property     | Type    | Description                                                                         |
| ------------ | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `collection` | String  | The collection slug used for admin authentication.                                  |
| `enabled`    | Boolean | Enable the admin dashboard (set by `cequre init` / `cequre add --plugins adminUi`). |
| `title`      | String  | Branding title rendered in the admin auth shell and header.                         |
| `logo`       | String  | Branding logo path rendered in the admin auth shell and header.                     |

The admin UI authenticates via an **HttpOnly `cequre_auth` cookie** set by the server (no client-accessible access/refresh tokens). A public `GET /api/_admin` endpoint exposes the `adminUi` branding so the login page can render before authentication. The admin collection is a sealed plane — user plugin hooks and DSL rules never touch it.

The admin UI is an **admin-only console**: it has no schema viewer or editor and exposes no developer surfaces. Schema design stays in the CLI, editor tooling, and `.cequre` files.

## `apiPrefix`

A shorthand for `core.api.prefix`:

```cequre
config {
  apiPrefix: "/api"
}
```

## `migrate`

```cequre
config {
  migrate: {
    dropOrphan: true
  }
}
```

| Property     | Type    | Description                                                                    |
| ------------ | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `dropOrphan` | Boolean | Drop orphaned tables and columns during `db:sync` without requiring `--force`. |

## `output`

Controls where generated files are written. The path is relative to the `cequre/` directory:

```cequre
config {
  output: "../src/generated"
}
```

If not specified, generated files go to `cequre/` (schema.json, gen.ts) and the project root (`cequre-types.ts`).

## Complete Example

```cequre
config {
  core: {
    api: {
      prefix: "/api"
      maxBodyBytes: 1048576
      trustedProxies: ["127.0.0.1"]
    }
    openapi: {
      enabled: true
    }
  }

  security: {
    auth: {
      strategies: ["jwt", "session"]
      jwt: {
        accessTokenExpiry: env("JWT_EXPIRY", "15m")
        refreshTokenExpiry: "7d"
        cookies: {
          name: "cequre_auth"
          timeout: "7d"
          refreshToken: true
          secure: true
          httpOnly: true
          sameSite: "lax"
          domain: "example.com"
        }
      }
      passwordPolicy: {
        minLength: 8
        requireUppercase: true
        requireNumber: true
      }
      lockout: {
        maxAttempts: 5
        durationMinutes: 15
      }
    }
    cors: {
      origin: ["http://localhost:3000"]
      credentials: true
    }
    rateLimit: {
      write: { max: 100, window: "15m" }
      login: { max: 5, window: "15m" }
    }
    headers: { enabled: true }
    secrets: { enabled: true }
    audit: { enabled: false }
    csrfTrustedOrigins: ["https://myapp.com"]
  }

  monitoring: {
    enabled: true
    apiKey: env("MONITORING_API_KEY")
    healthCheck: {
      enabled: true
      path: "/health"
      requiresAuth: false
    }
    requestId: { enabled: true }
  }

  adminUi: {
    collection: "users",
    title: "My App Admin"
    logo: "/logo.svg"
  }
}
```


# ==========================================
# File: core/database-sync.mdx
# ==========================================

# Database Sync

Cequre syncs your database directly from the compiled schema — no migration files, no version numbers, no `up`/`down` scripts. Run `cequre db:sync` and the runtime diffs your schema against the live database, then applies the changes.

## How It Works

![Database Sync Architecture](/database_sync_diagram.jpg)

<steplist>
  <step><code>cequre db:sync</code> loads <code>node_modules/.cequre/schema.json</code> (produced by <code>cequre generate</code>)</step>
  <step>Connects to the database using <code>DATABASE_URL</code></step>
  <step>Introspects the current database schema (tables, columns)</step>
  <step>Computes a diff between the compiled schema and the live database</step>
  <step>Applies non-destructive changes automatically</step>
  <step>Applies destructive changes only with <code>--force</code></step>
</steplist>

## Supported Databases

The adapter is selected based on the `DATABASE_URL` scheme:

| URL Scheme | Database | Adapter |
|---|---|---|
| `file:`, `sqlite:` | SQLite | `SQLiteAdapter` from `cequre-ts` |
| `postgres:`, `postgresql:` | PostgreSQL | `PostgresAdapter` from `cequre-ts` |
| `http:`, `https:` | SurrealDB | `SurrealDBAdapter` from `cequre-ts` |

All adapters ship in the embedded runtime (`cequre-ts`) — no separate driver packages are installed. The CLI dynamically resolves the adapter class based on the URL scheme.

## The Diff Report

After comparing the schema against the database, `db:sync` prints a report:

```
📊 Comparing schema against database...

  + Tables to create:
      + todos
      + products
  + Columns to add:
      + users.role
      + users.avatar
  - Tables to drop:
      - legacy_table
  - Columns to drop:
      - users.legacyField
```

### Change Types

| Type | Destructive? | Default | With `--force` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Create table** — collection doesn't exist in DB | No | ✅ Applied | ✅ Applied |
| **Add column** — field doesn't exist in table | No | ✅ Applied | ✅ Applied |
| **Drop table** — DB table not in schema (orphaned) | Yes | ⏭️ Skipped | ✅ Applied |
| **Drop column** — DB column not in schema (orphaned) | Yes | ⏭️ Skipped | ✅ Applied |

## Safe Mode (Default)

Without `--force`, the sync only applies **additive** changes:

```bash
cequre db:sync
```

- ✅ Creates missing tables
- ✅ Adds missing columns
- ⏭️ Skips dropping orphaned tables
- ⏭️ Skips dropping orphaned columns

This is safe to run in production — it never destroys data.

## Altering Existing Columns

By default the sync only adds missing columns — if you change an existing
field's **type** (e.g. `text` → `number`) or **requiredness** (e.g. required →
optional), the database column is left untouched. Enable shape convergence with
the `migrate` block:

```cequre
config {
  migrate {
    alterColumns: true;
  }
}
```

With `alterColumns: true`:

- **PostgreSQL** alters the column in place (`ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE`, `SET/DROP NOT NULL`).
- **SQLite / Turso** rebuild the table (new table → copy rows → drop old → rename), preserving your data.
- Changing a column from required to optional drops `NOT NULL` — rows can then be created/updated without that field.
- Changing a column from optional to required still errors out if existing rows contain `NULL` — fix the data first, then re-run the sync.
- **Adding or removing `@unique`** on an existing column is converged: PostgreSQL emits `ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE` / `DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS ...`, and SQLite/Turso rebuild the table with the new constraint. No more silent no-ops.
- **Adding `@index`** to an existing field requires a sync run — the `CREATE INDEX` is emitted when the table is (re)created.
- SurrealDB and MongoDB are schemaless — nothing to alter there.

**Production note:** the runtime's auto-sync never alters existing columns
when `NODE_ENV=production` — shape changes are applied only when you
explicitly run `cequre db:sync`.

## Force Mode

With `--force`, the sync also applies destructive changes:

```bash
cequre db:sync --force
```

- ✅ Creates missing tables
- ✅ Adds missing columns
- ✅ Drops orphaned tables
- ✅ Drops orphaned columns

In production (`NODE_ENV=production`), destructive changes are always skipped unless `--force` is explicitly provided, even if `--force` would normally apply them.

## System Tables

The sync preserves certain system tables that are not defined in the schema:

| Table | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `cequre_migrations` | Internal migration tracking |
| `cequre_refresh_tokens` | JWT refresh token storage |
| `cequre_audit_log` | Audit log entries (auto-created when `security.audit.enabled` is true) |

These tables are never dropped, even if they appear orphaned.

## Auto-Injected Collections

When `security.audit.enabled` is `true`, the compiler automatically injects a `cequre_audit_log` collection into the schema with these fields:

| Field | Type | Optional |
|---|---|---|
| `action` | `text` | No |
| `collection` | `text` | Yes |
| `recordId` | `text` | Yes |
| `userId` | `text` | Yes |
| `metadata` | `json` | Yes |
| `hmac` | `text` | No |
| `prevHmac` | `text` | Yes |

The HMAC fields create a tamper-evident chain — each log entry signs the previous entry's HMAC, so any modification is detectable.

## Workflow

```bash
# 1. Edit your .cequre files
# Add a new field to a collection:
#   collection products {
#     fields: {
#       + sku: text @unique
#     }
#   }

# 2. Recompile
cequre generate

# 3. Sync the database
cequre db:sync
# Output:
#   + Columns to add:
#       + products.sku
#   ⚙️  Applying changes...
#   ✅ Schema sync complete.

# 4. If you removed a field and want to drop the column:
cequre db:sync --force
```

## Environment Variables

`db:sync` automatically loads `.env` from the project root if it exists:

```bash
# .env
DATABASE_URL=file:./cequre.sqlite
# or
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/mydb
```

For SurrealDB, additional environment variables are used:

```bash
SURREAL_USER=root
SURREAL_PASS=root
SURREAL_NS=test
SURREAL_DB=test
```

## Related

- [CLI Reference](./cli-reference) — All CLI commands
- [Code Generation](./cli-reference) — What `schema.json` contains
- [Config Block](./config-block) — The `migrate` config option

# ==========================================
# File: core/decorators.mdx
# ==========================================

# Decorators

Decorators are metadata annotations attached to field definitions. They start with `@` and can take optional arguments in parentheses. Multiple decorators can be chained on a single field.

## Syntax

```cequre
fieldName: type @decorator
fieldName: type @decorator("arg")
fieldName: type @decorator1 @decorator2
```

Decorators also apply to defined-object fields — place them after the closing `}` (and any `[]` array suffix):

```cequre
meta: {
  key: text
  value: number
}[] @optional
```

## Available Decorators

### `@unique`

Ensures the field value is unique across all records in the collection. Creates a unique constraint in the database.

```cequre
email: email @unique
```

### `@optional`

Marks the field as nullable. By default, all fields are required. Use `@optional` to allow null values.

```cequre
bio: text @optional
metadata: json @optional
```

In the generated TypeScript types, optional fields get the `?` modifier:

```typescript
interface Users {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  bio?: string;      // optional
  metadata?: any;     // optional
}
```

### `@default`

Sets a default value for the field when no value is provided at create time. Takes a single argument (string, number, boolean, or identifier).

```cequre
role: text @default("user")
completed: boolean @default(false)
priority: select("low", "medium", "high") @default("medium")
viewCount: integer @default(0)
```

In the generated TypeScript `Create` input types, fields with a `@default` are optional (since the runtime will fill in the default):

```typescript
interface TodosCreate {
  title: string;
  completed?: boolean;   // has @default(false)
  author: string;
}
```

### `@hidden`

Hides the field from API responses. The field is still stored in the database and can be used in hooks and access rules, but it is stripped from JSON responses.

```cequre
internalNotes: text @hidden
```

### `@omit`

Prevents the field from being accepted in API mutations (Create/Update). The field is removed from OpenAPI input schemas, and any value passed in the request body is silently stripped.

```cequre
score: integer @omit
```

### `@index`

Creates a database index on the field to improve query performance. Use on fields that are frequently filtered or sorted.

```cequre
email: email @unique @index
status: select("draft", "published") @index
```

The index is created when the collection's table is created (and on table rebuilds for SQLite/Turso). Adding `@index` to an existing field requires a `cequre db:sync` run.

### `@encrypt`

Encrypts the field value at rest using AES-256-GCM. The value is encrypted before storage and transparently decrypted on read — your application code never sees the ciphertext. Requires `security.secrets.enabled` in the config and a `CEQURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` environment variable (see [Security](./security)).

```cequre
ssn: text @encrypt
diagnosis: text @encrypt
```

**Supported types:** `@encrypt` is only valid on **text-family** fields — `text`, `textarea`, `email`, `password`, `url`, `select`. Ciphertext is stored as a string (`enc:v1:...`), so non-text columns (boolean, number, integer, date, multiselect) and JSONB/array columns (json, object, array, richtext, upload) reject it at insert time. The CLI rejects these combinations at compile time.

**Restrictions (rejected at compile time):**

- `@encrypt` + `@unique` — the random IV per encryption means the same plaintext never produces the same ciphertext, so a UNIQUE constraint can never fire. Add a separate deterministic hash column (e.g. `ssnHash`) and mark that `@unique` instead.
- `@encrypt` + `@saveToJWT` — JWTs are base64, not encrypted; the plaintext would be embedded in every token.
- `@encrypt` on an auth collection's `email` field — register/login lookups compare plaintext against ciphertext and would never match.

**Fail-closed:** if `secrets.enabled` is `true` but the encryption key is missing, the server **fails to start** with a clear error — it never silently stores plaintext.

### `@title`

Designates the field as the primary human-readable title or label for records in the collection. The admin UI uses this field to display record names in relationship dropdowns, list views, and page headers instead of showing raw IDs.

```cequre
collection posts {
  fields {
    headline: text @title;
    author: relationship -> users;
  }
}
```

**Rules & Constraints:**
- **At most one per entity:** Only one field per collection or global may carry `@title`.
- **Readable fields only:** Cannot be combined with `@hidden`, `@omit`, or applied to `password` fields.
- **Top-level only:** Must be placed on a top-level field, not nested inside object/array subfields.

## Combining Decorators

Decorators can be freely combined. Order does not matter:

```cequre
email: email @unique @index
apiKey: text @unique @hidden
bio: text @optional @default("")
```

## Decorator Arguments

Decorators can take arguments in parentheses:

```cequre
role: text @default("user")
```

The argument value follows the same value rules as any DSL value:

| Argument Type | Example |
|---|---|
| String | `@default("user")` |
| Number | `@default(0)` |
| Boolean | `@default(false)` |

## Summary

| Decorator | Effect | Database Impact |
|---|---|---|
| `@unique` | Enforces uniqueness | Creates `UNIQUE` constraint |
| `@optional` | Allows null values | Column is `NULL`-able |
| `@default(value)` | Sets default value on create | Column gets `DEFAULT` clause |
| `@title` | Primary display label for records in Admin UI & relations | None |
| `@hidden` | Strips from API responses | None |
| `@omit` | Strips from Create/Update requests | None |
| `@index` | Adds database index | Creates `INDEX` |
| `@encrypt` | Encrypts value at rest (AES-256-GCM) | Stores `enc:v1:...` ciphertext |

## Related

- [Field Types](./field-types) — All available field types
- [Collections](./collections) — Where fields are defined
- [CLI Reference](./cli-reference) — How decorators affect generated TypeScript

This code defines a `calculateCircleArea` function that calculates the area of a circle based on the given radius. It then uses this function to calculate the area of a circle with a radius of 5 and prints the result to the console. The code includes comments and input error handling to ensure robust execution.

```javascript
function calculateCircleArea(radius) {
  // The code that calculate the area over a the given radius.
  return radius * radius * Math.PI;
}

if (calculateCircleArea(5) > 50) {
  return circleArea * 5;
}

// The code includes comments and input handling.
console.log("Circle Area:", result);
```

# ==========================================
# File: core/dsl-syntax.mdx
# ==========================================

# DSL Syntax

The Cequre DSL is a declarative language for defining backend schemas and configuration. This page covers the complete grammar — tokens, block structure, value types, and comments.

## File Convention

Cequre DSL files use the `.cequre` extension and live in the `cequre/` directory of your project. You can split your schema across multiple files — the compiler merges them:

```
cequre/
  config.cequre         # config {} block
  users.cequre          # collection users { ... }
  todos.cequre          # collection todos { ... }
  settings.cequre       # global settings { ... }
```

All `.cequre` files in the `cequre/` directory (including subdirectories) are discovered and compiled together.

## Top-Level Blocks

A `.cequre` file contains zero or more top-level blocks in any order:

```cequre
config {
  // framework-wide configuration
}

collection <name> {
  // a data collection (table/document)
}

global <name> {
  // a singleton document (e.g. site settings)
}
```

- **`config`** — appears once across all files. Defines security, monitoring, API prefix, etc.
- **`collection <name>`** — defines a data model. The name becomes the database table and API route.
- **`global <name>`** — defines a singleton document. Useful for site-wide settings.

## Properties

Inside each block, you write **properties** as key-value pairs:

```cequre
propertyName: value
```

Property names can be identifiers (`name`, `email`) or keywords used as property names (`config`, `collection`, `fields`). Values can be:

### Value Types

| Value | Syntax | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **String** | `"..."` | `"hello world"` |
| **Number** | integer or decimal | `42`, `-3.14` |
| **Boolean** | `true` / `false` | `true` |
| **Identifier** | bare word | `text`, `boolean` |
| **Function call** | `name(args)` | `relationship("users")`, `select("low", "high")` |
| **Array** | `[a, b, c]` | `["jwt", "session"]` |
| **Object** | `{ key: value }` | `{ enabled: true, path: "/health" }` |
| **Environment** | `env("VAR", default)` | `env("JWT_EXPIRY", "15m")` |

### Examples

```cequre
// String
prefix: "/api"

// Number
maxBodyBytes: 1048576

// Boolean
enabled: true

// Identifier (field type)
title: text

// Function call (field type with arguments)
author: relationship("users")

// Array
strategies: ["jwt", "session"]

// Object (nested block)
jwt: {
  accessTokenExpiry: "15m"
  refreshTokenExpiry: "7d"
}

// Environment variable with default
accessTokenExpiry: env("JWT_EXPIRY", "15m")
```

## Array Suffix

Any value can be suffixed with `[]` to mark it as an array:

```cequre
tags: text[]         // array of text values
permissions: text[]   // array of strings
```

## Decorators

Decorators are metadata annotations attached to properties (typically fields). They start with `@`:

```cequre
email: email @unique
bio: text @optional
role: text @default("user")
status: text @unique @optional
```

Multiple decorators can be chained. See the [Decorators](./decorators) page for the full list.

## Comments

Line comments start with `//` and continue to the end of the line:

```cequre
// This is a comment
collection users {
  auth: true  // this collection has auth enabled
  fields: {
    name: text
    // email must be unique across all users
    email: email @unique
  }
}
```

Comments are preserved by the formatter and used as leading comments in the output.

## Related Pages

- [Config Block](./config-block) — All properties allowed inside `config {}`
- [Collections](./collections) — All properties allowed inside `collection {}`
- [Field Types](./field-types) — All field types and their usage
- [Decorators](./decorators) — `@unique`, `@optional`, `@default`, and more
- [Environment Variables](./environment-variables) — The `env()` function

# ==========================================
# File: core/editor-support.mdx
# ==========================================

# Editor Support

Cequre provides a Language Server (LSP) and VS Code extension for a first-class editing experience: real-time diagnostics, autocompletion, and code formatting.

## VS Code Extension

The `vscode-cequre` package provides a VS Code extension that launches the Cequre LSP. It activates for `.cequre` files and provides:

- **Diagnostics** — squiggly lines for lexing, parsing, and semantic errors
- **Autocompletion** — context-aware completions for keywords, field types, decorators, and config keys
- **Formatting** — format-on-save with consistent 2-space indentation
- **Cross-file validation** — errors in one file take other `.cequre` files into account (e.g., relationship targets)

## LSP Server

The LSP server is powered by the Cequre CLI and uses the `vscode-languageserver` protocol. You start it with:

```bash
cequre lsp
```

This runs on stdio — editors launch it automatically. You typically never run this manually.

## Diagnostics

The LSP provides three layers of diagnostics:

### 1. Lexing Errors

Reported immediately when the lexer cannot tokenise a character:

```
✖ Lexing errors:
  Unexpected character '!' at line 5, column 3
```

### 2. Parsing Errors

Reported when the token stream doesn't match the grammar:

```
✖ Parsing errors:
  Expecting token of type: "RCurly" but found "Identifier"
```

### 3. Semantic Errors

Reported after successful parsing, during compilation. The LSP scans all `.cequre` files in the workspace for cross-file context:

- **Unknown property** — a key not in the allowed set for its block
- **Unknown field type** — a type not in the allowed field type list
- **Duplicate collection** — two collections with the same name
- **Invalid relationship target** — `relationship("x")` where `x` doesn't exist
- **Missing select options** — `select()` with zero arguments

### Cross-File Validation

The LSP scans all `.cequre` files in the workspace to build cross-file context. This means:

- A `relationship("users")` in `posts.cequre` validates against the `users` collection defined in `users.cequre`
- Duplicate collection names are detected even when collections are in different files
- When you edit one file, diagnostics update across all open files

## Autocompletion

The LSP provides context-aware completions based on what you're typing:

### Structural Keywords

When typing at the block level (not after a `:`), you get completions for:

- `config`, `collection`, `global` — top-level block keywords
- `core`, `security`, `monitoring`, `adminUi`, `output` — config block keys
- `api`, `prefix`, `maxBodyBytes`, `trustedProxies` — nested config keys
- `auth`, `cors`, `rateLimit`, `headers`, `secrets`, `audit`, `csrfTrustedOrigins` — security keys
- `strategies`, `jwt`, `apiKey`, `passwordPolicy`, `lockout` — auth keys
- `enabled`, `apiKey`, `healthCheck`, `path`, `requiresAuth`, `requestId` — monitoring keys
- `fields` — collection field definition key

### Field Types

When typing after a `:` (in a field definition context), you get completions for all 15 field types with documentation:

- `text`, `textarea`, `richtext`, `email`, `password`
- `boolean`, `integer`, `number`, `date`
- `select`, `multiselect`, `enum`
- `relationship`, `json`, `array`, `upload`

Each completion includes a `detail` line (e.g., "Stored as TEXT") and documentation.

### Decorators

When typing after `@`, you get decorator completions:

- `@unique` — Ensure field is unique
- `@optional` — Mark field as optional
- `@default(value)` — Set a default value
- `@hidden` — Hide from API responses
- `@index` — Add database index

### `env()` Function

The `env` completion appears in field type contexts with documentation about the env variable resolution pattern.

## Formatting

The formatter uses the parser to produce consistent formatting:

- 2-space indentation
- Consistent property separator (no trailing commas/semicolons)
- Multi-line object blocks for nested objects
- Single-line for simple key-value pairs
- Comments preserved and aligned as leading comments

The formatter never formats broken code — if the input has lex or parse errors, the original text is returned unchanged.

### Format on Save

In VS Code, enable format-on-save in your settings:

```json
{
  "[cequre]": {
    "editor.formatOnSave": true
  }
}
```

## Related

- [DSL Syntax](./dsl-syntax) — The grammar the LSP validates against
- [Config Block](./config-block) — The keys the LSP autocompletes in `config {}`
- [Collections](./collections) — The keys the LSP autocompletes in `collection {}`

# ==========================================
# File: core/environment-variables.mdx
# ==========================================

# Environment Variables

Cequre supports referencing environment variables directly in the DSL using the `env()` function. This lets you keep secrets and environment-specific configuration out of your schema files.

## `env()` Function

The `env()` function takes two arguments:

```cequre
env("VARIABLE_NAME", "default_value")
```

| Argument | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Variable name | Yes | The environment variable name (string literal). |
| Default value | No | Fallback value if the env var is not set. Can be a string, number, or boolean. |

### Example

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    auth: {
      strategies: ["jwt"]
      jwt: {
        accessTokenExpiry: env("JWT_EXPIRY", "15m")
        refreshTokenExpiry: env("JWT_REFRESH_EXPIRY", "7d")
      }
      lockout: {
        maxAttempts: env("LOGIN_ATTEMPTS", 5)
        durationMinutes: env("LOCKOUT_DURATION", 15)
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## How It Compiles

When the compiler encounters `env("JWT_EXPIRY", "15m")`, it produces a special object in the compiled schema:

```json
{
  "accessTokenExpiry": {
    "$env": "JWT_EXPIRY",
    "$default": "15m"
  }
}
```

At runtime, the framework reads the `$env` key, looks up `process.env.JWT_EXPIRY`, and falls back to `$default` if the variable is not set.

## Common Environment Variables

| Variable | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | Database connection string | `file:./cequre.sqlite`, `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db` |
| `JWT_SECRET` | Secret key for JWT signing | Auto-generated by `cequre init` |
| `JWT_EXPIRY` | JWT access token expiry duration | `15m` |
| `JWT_REFRESH_EXPIRY` | JWT refresh token expiry duration | `7d` |
| `LOGIN_ATTEMPTS` | Max failed login attempts before lockout | `5` |
| `LOCKOUT_DURATION` | Account lockout duration in minutes | `15` |
| `SMTP_PASS` | SMTP password for email transport | `your-smtp-password` |
| `SURREAL_USER` | SurrealDB username | `root` |
| `SURREAL_PASS` | SurrealDB password | `root` |
| `SURREAL_NS` | SurrealDB namespace | `test` |
| `SURREAL_DB` | SurrealDB database name | `test` |

## `.env` File

The `cequre init` command creates a `.env` file with sensible defaults:

```bash
JWT_SECRET=<auto-generated-hex-string>
DATABASE_URL=file:cequre.sqlite
```

For other database adapters:

```bash
# PostgreSQL
DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:***@localhost:5432/cequre_app

# Redis
DATABASE_URL=redis://localhost:6379

# SurrealDB
DATABASE_URL=http://localhost:8000
```

The `cequre db:sync` command automatically loads `.env` if it exists in the project root.

## Using `env()` in Different Contexts

The `env()` function works anywhere a value is expected — not just in config:

```cequre
config {
  core: {
    api: {
      prefix: env("API_PREFIX", "/api")
    }
  }
  security: {
    cors: {
      origin: env("CORS_ORIGINS", "http://localhost:3000")
    }
  }
}
```

However, it is most commonly used in the `security` block for sensitive values that should differ between environments (development, staging, production).

## Validation

The compiler validates that `env()` receives at least one string argument:

```
env()           // Error: requires at least one argument
env(123)        // Error: first argument must be a string
env("VAR")      // OK — no default (null if unset)
env("VAR", "x") // OK — default is "x"
env("VAR", 5)   // OK — default is 5
env("VAR", true) // OK — default is true
```

## Related

- [Config Block](./config-block) — Where `env()` is most commonly used
- [CLI Reference](./cli-reference) — `db:sync` loads `.env` automatically

# ==========================================
# File: core/error-handling.mdx
# ==========================================

# Error Handling

Cequre features a robust, secure, and developer-friendly error handling framework. It catches unhandled exceptions, intercepts database constraints, and ensures your API consistently returns predictable JSON error responses.

## Standard Error Response

When an error occurs, Cequre formats the HTTP response into a standard `CequreErrorResponse` structure. 

```json
{
  "code": "BAD_REQUEST",
  "message": "Bad request",
  "statusCode": 400,
  "timestamp": "2026-07-07T08:00:00.000Z",
  "path": "/api/users"
}
```

This structure is guaranteed across all endpoints, whether the error was thrown manually or generated by an unhandled exception.

## The `CequreError` Class

To manually trigger an API error and control the HTTP status code, throw the `CequreError` class anywhere in your custom endpoints or hooks:

```ts
import { CequreError } from "@cequrebackends/cequre";

export default function myEndpoint(ctx) {
  if (!ctx.user) {
    throw new CequreError("You must be logged in", "UNAUTHORIZED", 401);
  }
}
```

### Static Helpers

`CequreError` provides static helpers for the most common HTTP status codes. These are highly recommended as they automatically set the correct `code` and `statusCode`:

```ts
// 400 Bad Request
throw CequreError.BadRequest("Invalid input data");

// 401 Unauthorized
throw CequreError.Unauthorized("Authentication required");

// 402 Payment Required
throw CequreError.SubscriptionRequired("Please upgrade your plan");

// 403 Forbidden
throw CequreError.Forbidden("You do not have permission");

// 404 Not Found
throw CequreError.NotFound("Record not found");

// 409 Conflict
throw CequreError.Conflict("This action conflicts with current state");

// 428 Precondition Required
throw CequreError.NotConfigured("Plugin is not configured");

// 429 Too Many Requests
throw CequreError.TooManyRequests("Rate limit exceeded");

// 501 Not Implemented
throw CequreError.NotImplemented("Feature coming soon");
```

## Database Constraints

Cequre's error handling framework automatically intercepts underlying database exceptions (e.g., PostgreSQL errors) via the active Database Adapter. It translates raw database constraints into human-readable messages and appropriate HTTP status codes without leaking database internals.

<steplist>
  <step>
    <strong>Foreign Key Violations (409 Conflict)</strong>
    <br/>
    If a relationship field references a missing record, Cequre catches the error and responds: 
    <br/>
    <code>The value "userId" references a non-existent record in "users".</code>
  </step>
  <step>
    <strong>Unique Constraints (409 Conflict)</strong>
    <br/>
    If a record violates an <code>@unique</code> field, it translates to:
    <br/>
    <code>A record with this "email" value already exists. Please use a different value.</code>
  </step>
  <step>
    <strong>Not Null Constraints (400 Bad Request)</strong>
    <br/>
    If a required field is missing data, Cequre returns:
    <br/>
    <code>The field "title" is required and cannot be empty.</code>
  </step>
</steplist>

## Production Safety

Cequre is designed to be safe by default. If a plain standard JavaScript `Error` is thrown, or an unhandled exception occurs (such as a typo or logic failure in a hook):

- **In Development:** Cequre will return the raw `error.message` in the API response to assist with debugging.
- **In Production:** (`NODE_ENV=production`) Cequre scrubs the error message. It will automatically return a generic message: `"An unexpected error occurred. Please try again later."` and an `"INTERNAL_ERROR"` code (500) to ensure stack traces and sensitive server information are never leaked to clients.

> [!TIP]
> If you explicitly throw a `CequreError` instance, its message will **always** be sent to the client, even in production. Use `CequreError` for user-facing errors, and standard `Error` objects for internal system errors.


# ==========================================
# File: core/field-types.mdx
# ==========================================

# Field Types

Cequre supports 15 field types. Each maps to a specific database column type and TypeScript type. You can also nest objects as field types.

## Scalar Types

| Type | SQL Storage | TypeScript | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `text` | `TEXT` | `string` | `name: text` |
| `textarea` | `TEXT` | `string` | `description: textarea` |
| `richtext` | `JSONB` | `any` | `body: richtext` |
| `email` | `TEXT` | `string` | `email: email @unique` |
| `password` | `TEXT` (hashed) | `string` | `password: password` |
| `boolean` | `BOOLEAN` | `boolean` | `completed: boolean @default(false)` |
| `integer` | `INTEGER` | `number` | `viewCount: integer` |
| `number` | `NUMERIC` | `number` | `price: number` |
| `date` | `TIMESTAMPTZ` | `string` | `publishedAt: date @optional` |

**`text` vs `textarea`** — Both store as `TEXT`. The difference is semantic: `textarea` signals the admin UI to render a multi-line input.

**`password`** — Hashed automatically on write (bcrypt/argon2). Omitted from the generated model interface and API responses, but included in the `Create` input type.

**`email`** — Validated against an email pattern on create/update.

**`date`** — Stored as `TIMESTAMPTZ`. Values are ISO 8601 strings in TypeScript.

## Selection Types

### `select`

Enumerated type with a fixed set of string options. Requires at least one option — the compiler errors on zero.

```cequre
status: select("draft", "published", "archived")
```

```typescript
// Generated TypeScript
status: "draft" | "published" | "archived"
```

### `multiselect`

Multiple string selections stored as `TEXT[]`.

```cequre
tags: multiselect("work", "personal", "urgent")
```

```typescript
tags: string[]
```

### Enum shorthand

An inline enum defined as an array literal. Same result as `select` but more concise for simple cases.

```cequre
role: ["admin", "user"] @default("user")
```

```typescript
role: "admin" | "user"
```

## Relationship Type

### `relationship`

A foreign key reference to another collection. The first argument is the target collection slug — it must exist, or the compiler produces a semantic error.

```cequre
author: relationship("users")
```

```typescript
// Base model (unpopulated):
author: string

// Populated model:
author: Users
```

Mark a relationship as an array with `[]`:

```cequre
tags: relationship("tags")[]
```

## Complex Types

| Type | SQL Storage | TypeScript | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `json` | `JSONB` | `any` | `metadata: json @optional` |
| `upload` | `JSONB` | `any` | `avatar: upload @optional` |
| `array` | `JSONB` | `any[]` | `tags: array` |

### Array Suffix (`[]`)
You can append `[]` to any primitive or nested object type to create an array of that type. This provides strong typings natively.

```cequre
scores: integer[]
devices: { name: string; ip: string; }[]
```

```typescript
// Generated TypeScript
scores: number[]
tags: string[]
```

### `json`

Stores arbitrary JSON data as `JSONB`. The generated TypeScript type defaults to `any` (or a generic `Record<string, any>` depending on compiler rules) since the shape is unconstrained.

```cequre
metadata: json @optional
```

```typescript
// Generated TypeScript
metadata?: any
```

### `upload`

Stores file metadata (path, size, MIME type) as JSON.

## Nested Object Fields

Fields can contain nested objects with their own field definitions. The nested object is stored as `JSONB`.

```cequre
collection products {
  fields: {
    name: text
    dimensions: {
      width: number
      height: number
      unit: text
    }
  }
}
```

```typescript
// Generated TypeScript
dimensions: { width: number; height: number; unit: string }
```

### Array of Objects

You can easily create an array of objects by simply appending the `[]` suffix after the object block closing brace.

```cequre
collection users {
  fields: {
    history: {
      action: text
      timestamp: date
    }[]
  }
}
```

```typescript
// Generated TypeScript
history: { action: string; timestamp: string }[]
```

### Defined Objects with Decorators

Defined-object fields support decorators like any other field — write them after the closing `}` (and any `[]` suffix):

```cequre
collection todos {
  fields: {
    definedObj: {
      label: text
      value: number
    }[] @optional
  }
}
```

The compiler marks object and array fields optional by default; the explicit `@optional` is accepted and preserved for readability.

## Auto-Generated Fields

Every collection automatically includes these — you never declare them:

| Field | TypeScript | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `string` (UUID) | Primary key, auto-generated |
| `createdAt` | `string` | ISO timestamp, set on creation |
| `updatedAt` | `string` | ISO timestamp, updated on every modification |

## Related

- [Decorators](./decorators) — `@unique`, `@optional`, `@default`, `@hidden`, `@index`
- [Collections](./collections) — Where fields are defined

# ==========================================
# File: core/globals.mdx
# ==========================================

# Globals

A `global` block defines a singleton document — a single instance of a data model, useful for site-wide settings, configuration, or feature flags. Unlike collections (which have many records), globals have exactly one record.

## Syntax

```cequre
global <name> {
  fields: {
    // field definitions
  }
}
```

The name must be a valid identifier and unique across all `.cequre` files.

## Allowed Properties

Globals support the same allowed properties as collections:

| Property | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `fields` | Object | Field definitions (same types as collections). |
| `auth` | Boolean | Not typically used on globals. |
| `cache` | Object | Caching settings. |
| `hooks` | Object | Lifecycle hooks. |
| `admin` | Object | Admin UI settings. |

## Example: Site Settings

```cequre
global siteSettings {
  fields: {
    siteName: text
    description: textarea
    maintenanceMode: boolean @default(false)
    maxUploadSize: integer @default(10485760)
    theme: select("light", "dark", "auto") @default("auto")
  }
}
```

## Generated Types

Globals produce the same TypeScript types as collections (model, create, update, where clause):

```typescript
export interface SiteSettings {
  id: string;
  siteName: string;
  description: string;
  maintenanceMode: boolean;
  maxUploadSize: number;
  theme: "light" | "dark" | "auto";
}

export interface SiteSettingsCreate {
  siteName: string;
  description: string;
  maintenanceMode?: boolean;
  maxUploadSize?: number;
  theme?: "light" | "dark" | "auto";
}

export type SiteSettingsUpdate = Partial<SiteSettingsCreate>;
```

Globals are also registered in the `Collections` type:

```typescript
export type Collections = {
  siteSettings: SiteSettings;
  // ...collections...
};
```

## Validation

Globals go through the same field validation as collections:

- Field types must be in the allowed set
- Relationship targets must exist
- `select` fields must have at least one option
- Duplicate global names produce an error

## Use Cases

- **Site settings** — site name, description, maintenance flags
- **Feature flags** — toggle features on/off globally
- **Theme configuration** — colors, logos, layout
- **Billing plans** — current plan, limits, renewal date
- **SEO metadata** — default title, description, social image

## Related

- [Collections](./collections) — Collections share the same field/decorator system
- [Field Types](./field-types) — All available field types
- [CLI Reference](./cli-reference) — How globals are represented in generated code

# ==========================================
# File: core/installation.mdx
# ==========================================

# Installation

Cequre is distributed as a standalone binary, making it fast and easy to install on your system.

## What's Included

The Cequre CLI is a fully self-contained standalone binary. It ships with:

- **The complete TypeScript runtime baked in** — the Bun adapter, security, monitoring, realtime, storage, and the generated-client SDK are compiled into the binary itself. The runtime does **not** need to be installed as a separate package.
- **Bundled database drivers** — `postgres`, `mongodb`, `surrealdb`, and `@libsql/client` are compiled in, so you never install them yourself.

When you scaffold a project (`cequre init` / `cequre dev`), the CLI extracts its embedded runtime into `cequre/_generated/runtime/` (a single bundled `cequre.js` plus its `cequre.d.ts` declarations) and wires a `cequre-ts` module alias (via `tsconfig.json` `paths`) that points at it. Your server code imports the runtime with a bare `cequre-ts` specifier:

```ts
import { createCequre } from "../_generated/server";
import { PostgresAdapter } from "cequre-ts";
```
