No `cequre-ts` dependency is required in a scaffolded project — the runtime version your CLI ships is the version you run.

## Operating System Support

Standalone binaries are built for the following platforms (see `deploy/distribution/`):

- 🍏 **macOS (arm64)** — `cequre-mac-arm64`
- 🐧 **Linux (amd64 / arm64)** — `cequre-linux-x64`, `cequre-linux-arm64` (via `bun run release:binaries`)
- 🪟 **Windows (amd64 / arm64)** — `cequre-windows-x64.exe`, `cequre-windows-arm64.exe`

Build all platform binaries with:

```bash
bun run release:binaries
```

## Editor Support (LSP)

The official VS Code extension (`vscode-cequre`) launches the Cequre LSP (`cequre lsp --stdio`) and provides syntax highlighting, autocompletion, and real-time schema validation for `.cequre` files.

## Next Steps

Check out the [Overview](./overview) and [Basic Usage](./basic-usage) guides to learn more about Cequre DSL, schema modeling, and plugins.


# ==========================================
# File: core/overview.mdx
# ==========================================

# Cequre.

Cequre is a schema-first backend framework that compiles `.cequre` files into a typed runtime, database schema, and CRUD API.

## How It Works

- Write `.cequre` files in the `cequre/` directory.
- Run `cequre generate` or `cequre dev` to parse them into a Universal AST.
- The AST lowers into a native runtime, currently Bun, with Go support planned.
- The runtime boots an API server with auth, realtime subscriptions, and generated endpoints.

## Design Philosophy

- **Language-agnostic core.** The DSL defines the schema and policies; the engine handles execution.
- **Schema as source of truth.** `.cequre` files are canonical, and generated files are not edited by hand.
- **No migration files.** `cequre db:sync` applies schema changes directly.
- **Configuration as code.** Security, rate limits, CORS, and monitoring are declared in the DSL.

## Key Features

- CRUD API for every collection.
- Authentication with JWT, session, or API key strategies.
- Access control rules written in TypeScript.
- Lifecycle hooks for create, update, and delete events.
- Realtime updates via WebSocket and Server-Sent Events.
- Caching with TTL and stale-while-revalidate support.
- Rate limiting per action.
- Auto-generated OpenAPI docs at `/api/docs`.
- Optional admin UI — a sealed, admin-only console with no developer or schema surfaces.
- Database sync with `cequre db:sync`.
- VS Code and LSP support.

## Example

```cequre
// cequre/schema/config.cequre
config {
  core: {
    api: {
      prefix: "/api"
    }
  }

  security: {
    auth: {
      strategies: ["jwt"]
      jwt: {
        accessTokenExpiry: "15m"
        refreshTokenExpiry: "7d"
      }
    }
  }

  monitoring: {
    healthCheck: {
      enabled: true
      path: "/health"
    }
  }
}
```

```cequre
// cequre/schema/collections.cequre
collection users {
  auth: true
  fields: {
    name: text
    email: email @unique
    password: password
    role: text @default("user")
  }
}

collection todos {
  fields: {
    title: text
    completed: boolean @default(false)
    author: relationship("users")
  }
}
```

## Generated Output

- `node_modules/.cequre/schema.json` — compiled Universal AST.
- `cequre/_generated/server.ts` — native entry point.
- `cequre-types.ts` — typed collection interfaces.

## Runtime

- REST endpoints are generated automatically.
- JWT auth is wired into `users`.
- Health checks are exposed at `/health`.
- OpenAPI docs are available at `/api/docs`.


# ==========================================
# File: core/project-structure.mdx
# ==========================================

# Project Structure

A Cequre project has a specific directory layout. This page explains what goes where and why.

## Directory Layout

```
my-app/
├── cequre/                    # Cequre backend (schema + runtime + generated + app code)
│   ├── schema/                # DSL files (source of truth)
│   │   ├── config.cequre      # Framework configuration
│   │   ├── collections.cequre # Collection definitions (can be split)
│   │   └── globals.cequre     # Global definitions (optional)
│   ├── index.ts               # Server entry point — composition root (starts the server)
│   ├── routes.ts              # Custom routes module (CequreModule)
│   └── _generated/            # Compiler output (generated, don't edit)
│       ├── runtime/           # Embedded runtime bundle (extracted by the CLI)
│       │   ├── cequre.js      # Single bundled runtime file
│       │   └── cequre.d.ts    # Its TypeScript declarations
│       ├── server.ts          # Runtime SDK entry point with createCequre()
│       ├── client.ts          # Client SDK
│       └── schemas.ts         # TypeBox schemas
├── public/                     # Static assets
│   └── index.html              # Landing page
├── .env                        # Environment variables
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.json               # Maps `cequre-ts` → ./cequre/_generated/runtime/cequre
```

## The `cequre/schema/` Directory

This is where your `.cequre` DSL files live. The compiler discovers all `.cequre` files recursively in this directory.

### Splitting Schema Files

You can split your schema across multiple files. The compiler merges them:

```
cequre/schema/
  config.cequre          # config {} block
  users.cequre           # collection users { ... }
  posts.cequre            # collection posts { ... }
  comments.cequre        # collection comments { ... }
  settings.cequre        # global siteSettings { ... }
```

Each file can contain any number of top-level blocks. The only constraint is that `config {}` should appear once across all files.

### Generated Artifacts in `cequre/_generated/`

Generated by `cequre generate` alongside your `.cequre` files:

- `node_modules/.cequre/schema.json` — the compiled schema as JSON
- `cequre/_generated/runtime/` — the embedded runtime bundle, extracted from the CLI binary on scaffold
- `cequre/_generated/server.ts` — the runtime SDK entry point with `createCequre()`
- `cequre/_generated/client.ts` — the client SDK

The `runtime/` directory contains the compiled (minified) Cequre runtime as a **single bundled file** (`cequre.js`) plus its TypeScript declarations (`cequre.d.ts`). Your `tsconfig.json` maps the bare `cequre-ts` import specifier to `./cequre/_generated/runtime/cequre`, so runtime imports in your server code (`import { createCequre } from "cequre-ts"`) resolve to the version your CLI shipped.

Never edit these files — they are overwritten on every build.

## The `cequre/` Directory (Application Code)

Your TypeScript application code lives directly in `cequre/` alongside the schema and generated output. Two files make up the scaffolded app.

### `index.ts`

The server entry point — the **composition root**. This is the only file that calls `app.start()`. It creates the Cequre app instance (adapter + plugins), registers the `routesModule`, and boots the server:

```typescript
import { createCequre } from "./_generated/server";
import { PostgresAdapter, defaultSecurity, defaultMonitoring } from "cequre-ts";
import { routesModule } from "./routes";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new PostgresAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
  plugins: [defaultSecurity(), defaultMonitoring()],
}).use(routesModule);

app.start({ port: process.env.PORT ? parseInt(process.env.PORT) : 3000 }).catch(console.error);
```

> [!TIP]
> The scaffold wires routes through a `CequreModule`. For app-scoped code you can also skip the module and register directly on the exported `app` — see [App Patterns](./app-patterns) for when each style fits.

### `routes.ts`

Custom routes module — a `CequreModule` that registers routes beyond the auto-generated CRUD endpoints. It also ships with a root `/` index route and a `/health` health check:

```typescript
import { CequreModule, t } from "cequre-ts";
import type { Collections } from "./_generated/server";

export const routesModule = new CequreModule<Collections>();

// Default root index page serving from public directory
routesModule.get("/", () => {
  return new Response(Bun.file("public/index.html"));
});

// Basic health check for uptime monitoring and container probes
routesModule.get("/health", () => {
  return new Response(JSON.stringify({ status: "ok", timestamp: new Date().toISOString() }), {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  });
});

// Custom routes
routesModule.get("/greeting", () => ({ greeting: "hello from cequre" }), {
  response: t.Object({
    greeting: t.String(),
  }),
});
```

The `CequreModule` collects its registrations (`access`, `hooks`, `cron`, and `get`/`post`/`put`/`patch`/`delete` routes) and applies them to the app when `.use(module)` is called from the composition root. The route methods (`get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`) are fully typed — each accepts `(path, handler, options)` or `(path, options, handler)` overloads, and `handler` is typed against your `Collections` schema.

### Adding hooks or access rules

You can register hooks and access-control rules on the same `routesModule` (or create additional `CequreModule` files and `.use()` them). For example, hooks:

```typescript
routesModule.hooks("todos", {
  beforeCreate: async (ctx) => {
    if (!ctx.data.author) ctx.data.author = ctx.user?.id || "anonymous";
    return ctx.data;
  },
  afterCreate: async (ctx) => {
    console.log("Todo created:", ctx.data.id);
  },
});
```

And access rules:

```typescript
routesModule.access("users", {
  read: (ctx) => ctx.user?.role === "admin" || ctx.user?.id === ctx.doc?.id,
  create: (ctx) => true,
  update: (ctx) => ctx.user?.role === "admin" || ctx.user?.id === ctx.doc?.id,
  delete: (ctx) => ctx.user?.role === "admin",
});
```

## The `public/` Directory

Static assets served by the Bun server. The initial `cequre generate` scaffold creates a landing page at `public/index.html`.

## `cequre/_generated/` (TypeScript types & SDK)

Generated TypeScript types and the client SDK live under `cequre/_generated/`. Types for your collections and globals are exported from `cequre/_generated/server.ts`, so you import them relative to your app code:

```typescript
import type { Todos, TodosCreate, TodosWhereClause } from "./_generated/server";
```

Never edit these files — they are overwritten on every build.

## `.env`

Environment variables. Created by the initial `cequre generate` scaffold with:

```bash
JWT_SECRET=<auto-generated>
DATABASE_URL=file:./temp/cequre.sqlite
```

Loaded automatically by `cequre db:sync` and by the runtime.

## `package.json`

The initial scaffold creates a `package.json` with build/run scripts. Because the runtime is embedded and aliased via `tsconfig.json`, scaffolded projects typically have **no `cequre-ts` dependency** — the runtime comes from the CLI:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "cequre dev -e cequre/index.ts",
    "build": "bun build cequre/index.ts --outdir dist --target bun",
    "start": "NODE_ENV=production bun run dist/index.js"
  }
}
```

The `tsconfig.json` alias is what makes `import { createCequre } from "cequre-ts"` resolve to the embedded runtime:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "types": ["bun", "node"],
    "paths": {
      "cequre-ts": ["./cequre/_generated/runtime/cequre"]
    }
  }
}
```

## What Gets Generated vs What You Write

| File | Who Writes It | Can You Edit It? |
|---|---|---|
| `cequre/schema/*.cequre` | `cequre init` creates `config.cequre`, then **you** | ✅ Yes — this is the source of truth |
| `node_modules/.cequre/schema.json` | `cequre generate` | ❌ No — generated |
| `cequre/_generated/runtime/` | CLI (extracted from the binary) | ❌ No — generated |
| `cequre/_generated/server.ts` | `cequre generate` | ❌ No — generated |
| `cequre/_generated/client.ts` | `cequre generate` | ❌ No — generated |
| `cequre/_generated/schemas.ts` | `cequre generate` | ❌ No — generated |
| `cequre/index.ts` | `cequre init` (initial scaffold), then **you** | ✅ Yes |
| `cequre/routes.ts` | `cequre init` (initial scaffold), then **you** | ✅ Yes |
| `.env` | `cequre init` (initial scaffold), then **you** | ✅ Yes |
| `tsconfig.json` | CLI (adds the `cequre-ts` path alias) | ✅ Yes |

## Related

- [CLI Reference](./cli-reference) — Commands that create and build this structure
- [App Patterns](./app-patterns) — Exported app vs `CequreModule`: choosing how to organize code
- [Database Sync](./database-sync) — How `schema.json` drives database changes

# ==========================================
# File: core/security.mdx
# ==========================================

# Security

Cequre includes a comprehensive security subsystem covering authentication, encryption, audit logging, rate limiting, and vulnerability management. This page documents every security feature with configuration examples.

## Authentication

Cequre supports three authentication strategies: JWT, API keys, and MFA/TOTP. They can be combined — for example, JWT with MFA enforcement for admin roles.

### JWT Authentication

JWT is the default auth strategy. It uses HS256 signing via the `jose` library with access + refresh token rotation.

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    auth: {
      strategies: ["jwt"]
      jwt: {
        accessTokenExpiry: "15m"
        refreshTokenExpiry: "7d"
        cookies: {
          name: "cequre_auth"
          secure: true
          httpOnly: true
          sameSite: "strict"
          refreshToken: true
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `accessTokenExpiry` | `"15m"` | Access token lifetime |
| `refreshTokenExpiry` | `"7d"` | Refresh token lifetime |
| `cookies.name` | `"cequre_auth"` | Cookie name for access token |
| `cookies.secure` | `false` | Set `Secure` attribute |
| `cookies.httpOnly` | `false` | Set `HttpOnly` attribute |
| `cookies.sameSite` | `"lax"` | SameSite policy (`lax`, `strict`, `none`) |
| `cookies.refreshToken` | `false` | Also set refresh token cookie |

Refresh tokens are rotated on every use — the old token is revoked and a new pair is issued. Tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes, never raw.

#### JWT Secret Rotation

To rotate your JWT secret without invalidating active sessions, set both the new and old secret during a transition period:

```bash
# .env
JWT_SECRET="new-secret-value-here"
JWT_PREVIOUS_SECRET="old-secret-value-here"
```

New tokens are signed with `JWT_SECRET`. Existing tokens are verified against `JWT_SECRET` first, then `JWT_PREVIOUS_SECRET` as fallback. Once all old tokens have expired, remove `JWT_PREVIOUS_SECRET`.

#### Email Verification (`verify_email` & `resend_if_expire`)

Require users to verify their email address before accessing protected routes or logging in:

```cequre
collection users {
  auth: true
  emails: {
    verify_email: true
    resend_if_expire: true
  }
}
```

- **Session Token Suppression**: Registration (`POST /api/<slug>/register`) creates the user record with `_verified: false` and suppresses issuing JWT tokens or cookies until the email is verified.
- **Login Enforcement**: Unverified users attempting to log in receive a `403 Forbidden` error with `{ "error": "Email verification required. Please verify your email before logging in." }`.
- **Automatic Resend on Expiry (`resend_if_expire: true`)**: If enabled, unverified login attempts or expired link submissions automatically issue and email a fresh signed verification link. Expired tokens undergo HMAC signature validation to prevent token spoofing.
- **Manual Resend Endpoint**: Users can request a new verification link anytime via `POST /api/<slug>/resend-verification` with `{ "email": "user@example.com" }`.

The `_verified`, `_verificationToken`, and MFA fields are server-managed: the CLI injects them with `hidden` + `omit`, so they are stripped from client payloads and from every API response. Internal auth flows (login, MFA challenge, verification) read them via an `includeHidden: true` opt-in — a server-side flag that HTTP callers cannot set.

### Default Password Stripping (`includePassword`)

Fields defined with `type: "password"` are automatically stripped from all read operation outputs across REST and Local API queries by default.

- **REST Endpoints**: Public HTTP REST requests (`GET /api/<slug>` or `GET /api/<slug>/:id`) ignore/strip `includePassword` query parameters to prevent password hash leakage over HTTP.
- **Local API Opt-In**: In server-side TypeScript code (`ctx.cequre.find` or `app.findById`), pass `{ includePassword: true }` to retrieve raw password hashes when performing low-level operations.

### API Key Authentication

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    auth: {
      apiKey: {
        enabled: true
        header: "x-api-key"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

API keys are stored as SHA-256 hashes in the `cequre_api_keys` system table. Verification uses timing-safe comparison.

Generate an API key:

```bash
bun run gen:key
```

Example API request with an API key:

```bash
curl -H "x-api-key: rak_xxxxxxxx" https://your-app/api/todos
```

### MFA / TOTP

Multi-factor authentication using RFC 6238 TOTP. Compatible with Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, and any standard TOTP app.

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    auth: {
      mfa: {
        enabled: true
        issuer: "My App"
        backupCodeCount: 10
        enforceForRoles: ["admin"]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `mfa.enabled` | `false` | Enable MFA endpoints |
| `mfa.issuer` | `"Cequre"` | Name shown in authenticator app |
| `mfa.backupCodeCount` | `10` | Number of single-use backup codes generated |
| `mfa.enforceForRoles` | `[]` | Roles that must enroll MFA before login |

#### MFA Enrollment Flow

1. User authenticates and calls the enroll endpoint:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  https://your-app/api/users/mfa/enroll
```

Response includes a `secret`, `otpauthUri` (for QR codes), and one-time `backupCodes`:

```json
{
  "secret": "JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP",
  "otpauthUri": "otpauth://totp/My%20App:user%40example.com?secret=...",
  "backupCodes": ["a1b2c-3d4e5-f6g7h8", ...],
  "message": "Scan the QR code with your authenticator app, then verify with a code to complete enrollment."
}
```

2. User scans the QR code, then verifies with their first TOTP code:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"mfaCode": "123456"}' \
  https://your-app/api/users/mfa/verify
```

3. Future logins return an MFA challenge:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"user@example.com","password":"secret"}' \
  https://your-app/api/users/login
```

```json
{
  "mfaRequired": true,
  "mfaToken": "eyJhbGci..."
}
```

4. Complete the login with a TOTP code or backup code:

```bash
# With TOTP code
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"mfaToken":"eyJ...","mfaCode":"123456"}' \
  https://your-app/api/users/mfa/login

# With backup code
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"mfaToken":"eyJ...","mfaCode":"skip","backupCode":"a1b2c-3d4e5-f6g7h8"}' \
  https://your-app/api/users/mfa/login
```

5. Disable MFA (requires current TOTP code):

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"mfaCode":"123456"}' \
  https://your-app/api/users/mfa/disable
```

**MFA endpoints:**

| Endpoint | Auth | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `POST /:collection/mfa/enroll` | Bearer token | Generate secret + backup codes |
| `POST /:collection/mfa/verify` | Bearer token | Verify first TOTP code to complete enrollment |
| `POST /:collection/mfa/login` | MFA token | Complete login with TOTP or backup code |
| `POST /:collection/mfa/disable` | Bearer token | Disable MFA (requires current TOTP code) |

Backup codes are single-use, SHA-256 hashed, and consumed on use. Store them safely — they are shown only once during enrollment.

## Password Policy

Enforce password strength requirements on registration and password reset:

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    auth: {
      passwordPolicy: {
        minLength: 12
        requireUppercase: true
        requireNumber: true
      }
    }
  }
}
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `minLength` | — | Minimum password length |
| `requireUppercase` | `false` | Require at least one uppercase letter |
| `requireNumber` | `false` | Require at least one number |

## Account Lockout

Lock accounts after too many failed login attempts:

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    auth: {
      lockout: {
        maxAttempts: 5
        durationMinutes: 15
      }
    }
  }
}
```

After `maxAttempts` failed logins, the account is locked for `durationMinutes`. Failed attempts are tracked per `collection:email` and cleared on successful login.

## Encryption at Rest

Cequre supports AES-256-GCM field-level encryption. Mark any field with the `@encrypt` decorator and the value is automatically encrypted before storage and decrypted on read — transparent to your application code.

### Schema Example

```cequre
collection patients {
  fields {
    name: text
    ssn: text @encrypt
    diagnosis: text @encrypt
    ssnHash: text  // deterministic hash for lookups
  }
}
```

### Configuration

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    secrets: {
      enabled: true
    }
  }
}
```

Set the encryption key via environment variable:

```bash
export CEQURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY="your-32-character-minimum-key"
```

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `secrets.enabled` | Enable field-level encryption |
| `secrets.encryptionKey` | Env var name for the key (default: `CEQURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) |
| `CEQURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Encryption key (min 16 characters, recommended 32+) |

### How It Works

- **On write (create/update):** Fields marked with `@encrypt` are encrypted using AES-256-GCM with a random 12-byte IV per value. Ciphertext is stored as `enc:v1:<base64(iv)>:<base64(ciphertext)>`.
- **On read (find/findById):** Encrypted fields are automatically decrypted before returning to your code.
- **Key derivation:** The encryption key is derived from your passphrase using HKDF-SHA256 with a fixed label (`cequre-field-encryption-v1`), separating it from JWT and audit keys.

**Fail-closed:** if `secrets.enabled` is `true` but the encryption key is missing, the server **fails to start** with a clear error — it never silently stores plaintext. Set `CEQURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (or the custom env var from `secrets.encryptionKey`) before booting.

**Supported types:** `@encrypt` is only valid on text-family fields — `text`, `textarea`, `email`, `password`, `url`, `select`. The CLI rejects `@encrypt` on non-text types (boolean, number, integer, date, multiselect) and on JSONB/array types (json, object, array, richtext, upload), because ciphertext is a string that those columns cannot hold.

**Restrictions (rejected at compile time):** `@encrypt` cannot be combined with `@unique` (the random IV makes the constraint unenforceable — use a deterministic hash column like `ssnHash` instead), cannot be combined with `@saveToJWT` (the plaintext would be embedded in the JWT), and cannot be applied to an auth collection's `email` field (register/login lookups compare plaintext against ciphertext). See [Decorators](./decorators) for details.

**Important:** Encrypted fields are not queryable — you can't filter by an encrypted column. If you need to look up by an encrypted field, create a deterministic hash column (e.g. `ssnHash`) alongside it and filter on that instead.

## Audit Logging

Cequre's audit log is **tamper-evident** — each entry is HMAC-SHA256 chained to the previous entry, making silent modification detectable.

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    audit: {
      enabled: true
      retentionDays: 365
    }
  }
}
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `audit.enabled` | `false` | Enable audit logging |
| `audit.secret` | Derived from `JWT_SECRET` via HKDF | HMAC signing key |
| `audit.retentionDays` | Unlimited | Auto-delete entries older than N days |

Each CRUD operation (create, update, delete) is automatically logged with:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `action` | `create`, `update`, or `delete` |
| `collection` | Collection slug |
| `recordId` | Affected record ID |
| `userId` | User who triggered the action |
| `requestId` | Request ID for correlation with server logs |
| `metadata` | Operation data |
| `hmac` | HMAC-SHA256 of the entry + previous entry's HMAC |
| `prevHmac` | Previous entry's HMAC (chain link) |

### Audit Export

Export all audit entries with chain verification:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  https://your-app/api/audit/export
```

Response:

```json
{
  "exportedAt": "2026-07-06T12:00:00.000Z",
  "totalEntries": 42,
  "chainStatus": { "ok": true, "firstBadIndex": null },
  "entries": [...]
}
```

If `chainStatus.ok` is `false`, `firstBadIndex` indicates the first tampered entry.

### Manual Retention Cleanup

Trigger audit cleanup programmatically (in addition to the automatic 24h timer):

```typescript
const deleted = await runtime.purgeOldAuditEntries(90); // delete entries older than 90 days
console.log(`Deleted ${deleted} old audit entries`);
```

## Rate Limiting

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    rateLimit: {
      login: { max: 5, window: "15m" }
      write: { max: 100, window: "1m" }
    }
  }
}
```

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `rateLimit.login` | Rate limit for POST to `/login` and `/register` endpoints |
| `rateLimit.write` | Rate limit for POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE on all other endpoints |
| `max` | Maximum requests in the window |
| `window` | Time window: `"15m"`, `"1h"`, `"30s"` |

Rate limiting uses the configured KV store (memory, SQLite, or Redis) for distributed deployments. Client IP resolution respects [trusted proxies](#trusted-proxies).

Override the rate limit max via environment variable (for high-throughput deployments):

```bash
export RATE_LIMIT_MAX=1000
```

## Security Headers

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    headers: {
      enabled: true
      contentSecurityPolicy: "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'"
    }
  }
}
```

| Header | Value |
|--------|-------|
| `Content-Security-Policy` | Configurable (default: `default-src 'self'`) |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` |
| `Permissions-Policy` | `geolocation=(), microphone=(), camera=()` |
| `X-XSS-Protection` | `1; mode=block` |

Set `contentSecurityPolicy: false` to explicitly omit the CSP header. Set it to a custom string for fine-grained control:

```cequre
contentSecurityPolicy: "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'"
```

## CSRF Protection

CSRF protection is built-in and always active for state-changing requests (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) when cookies are present. It uses same-origin verification via Origin/Referer headers, with a custom header bypass for API clients.

```cequre
config {
  security: {
    csrfTrustedOrigins: ["https://your-frontend.com"]
  }
}
```

Requests with any of these headers bypass the origin check (for API clients that don't send cookies):
- `X-CEQURE-CSRF`
- `X-CSRF-Token`
- `X-Requested-With`

## Trusted Proxies

When behind a load balancer or reverse proxy, configure trusted proxy IPs so the rate limiter can safely use `X-Forwarded-For`:

```cequre
config {
  core: {
    api: {
      trustedProxies: ["10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2"]
    }
  }
}
```

When `trustedProxies` is set, `X-Forwarded-For` is only trusted if the direct connection IP is in the list. Otherwise, the direct connection IP is used.

## Secrets Management

Cequre abstracts secret resolution through a `SecretsProvider` interface, allowing production deployments to use KMS, HashiCorp Vault, or other external secret stores instead of environment variables.

### Default: Environment Variables

The default `EnvVarSecrets` provider reads from `process.env`. No configuration needed — this is how `JWT_SECRET`, `CEQURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, and `CEQURE_AUDIT_SECRET` are resolved today.

### Custom Provider

Implement the `SecretsProvider` interface for external secret stores:

```typescript
import { type SecretsProvider } from "cequre-ts";

class VaultSecrets implements SecretsProvider {
  async getSecret(name: string): Promise<string | null> {
    // Read from HashiCorp Vault
    const response = await fetch(`http://vault:8200/v1/secret/data/${name}`, {
      headers: { "X-Vault-Token": process.env.VAULT_TOKEN! },
    });
    if (!response.ok) return null;
    const data = await response.json();
    return data.data.data.value;
  }

  async listSecrets(): Promise<string[]> {
    // List available secrets
    return ["JWT_SECRET", "CEQURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY"];
  }
}
```

### Environment Variables Reference

| Variable | Required | Description |
|----------|----------|-------------|
| `JWT_SECRET` | Yes (JWT auth) | JWT signing secret |
| `JWT_PREVIOUS_SECRET` | No | Previous JWT secret for rotation grace period |
| `CEQURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Yes (encryption) | AES-256-GCM encryption key (min 16 chars) |
| `CEQURE_AUDIT_SECRET` | No | Audit HMAC key (defaults to HKDF from `JWT_SECRET`) |
| `RATE_LIMIT_MAX` | No | Override rate limit max threshold |

## SBOM & Dependency Auditing

Generate a Software Bill of Materials (CycloneDX 1.5 JSON):

```bash
bun run sbom
```

Output: `sbom/cequre-sbom-<timestamp>-cyclonedx.json` + `sbom/cequre-sbom-latest-cyclonedx.json`. Contains all workspace packages and external dependencies with Package URLs (`pkg:npm/name@version`).

Run a dependency vulnerability audit:

```bash
bun run audit
```

Exits non-zero if any high or critical vulnerabilities are found. Suitable for CI pipelines.

### CI Integration

Cequre includes a GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/security.yml`) that runs on every push to `main`, every PR, and weekly on Monday:

- Runs `bun run audit` — fails on high/critical CVEs
- Runs `bun run sbom` — generates SBOM artifact
- Uploads SBOM as a GitHub artifact (90-day retention)

Dependabot is configured (`.github/dependabot.yml`) for weekly npm and GitHub Actions dependency updates.

## Vulnerability Disclosure

See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/CodesOrdinate/cequre/blob/main/SECURITY.md) for the full vulnerability disclosure policy.

**Summary:**

| Step | Target |
|------|--------|
| Acknowledgement | 48 hours |
| Initial assessment | 5 business days |
| Fix or mitigation | 30 days (critical: 7 days) |
| Public disclosure | After fix, or 90 days (whichever comes first) |

**Do NOT open public GitHub issues for security vulnerabilities.** Use GitHub Security Advisories or email security@codesordinate.com.

## Webhook Signing

When sending outbound webhooks (e.g. notifying a third-party of events), sign the payload so consumers can verify authenticity.

```typescript
import { signWebhook, WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_HEADER } from "cequre-ts";

const payload = JSON.stringify({ event: "order.created", id: "123" });
const signature = await signWebhook(process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET!, payload);

// Send with the webhook request
fetch("https://partner.com/webhook", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    [WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_HEADER]: signature,
  },
  body: payload,
});
```

The signature header uses the format `X-Cequre-Signature: t=<timestamp>,v1=<hex-hmac>`.

Consumers verify the signature:

```typescript
import { verifyWebhookSignature } from "cequre-ts";

const valid = await verifyWebhookSignature(
  process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET!,
  request.headers.get("X-Cequre-Signature")!,
  rawBody,
  300, // 5 min tolerance
);
if (!valid) return new Response("Invalid signature", { status: 401 });
```

| Function | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `signWebhook(secret, payload)` | Signs a payload, returns `t=<ts>,v1=<hex>` |
| `verifyWebhookSignature(secret, header, payload, tolerance)` | Verifies with constant-time comparison (default 5 min tolerance) |
| `WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_HEADER` | `"X-Cequre-Signature"` |

Uses HMAC-SHA256 via Web Crypto. The timestamp prevents replay attacks — signatures older than the tolerance window are rejected.

## Idempotency Keys

Prevent duplicate side effects when clients retry requests. Send an `Idempotency-Key` header on any POST, PUT, or PATCH request:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: client-generated-uuid" \
  -d '{"amount": 100, "currency": "USD"}' \
  https://your-app/api/payments
```

The first request executes normally and the response is cached in the configured KV store (24-hour TTL). If the same `Idempotency-Key` is sent again, the cached response is returned with an `X-Idempotent-Replay: true` header — no duplicate side effect.

```bash
# Duplicate request — returns the original response
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: client-generated-uuid" \
  -d '{"amount": 100, "currency": "USD"}' \
  https://your-app/api/payments

# Response headers:
# X-Idempotent-Replay: true
```

Only successful responses (2xx) are cached. Error responses are not cached, allowing the client to retry with the same key after a failure.

Idempotency uses the same KV store as rate limiting (memory, SQLite, or Redis) — in multi-instance deployments, configure Redis-backed KV so idempotency works across instances.

## Field-Level Access Control

Control which roles can read or write specific fields. Configure on the field definition:

```swift
collection employees {
  fields {
    name: text
    email: text
    salary: number { readRoles: ["admin", "hr"], writeRoles: ["admin", "hr"] }
    department: text { readRoles: ["admin", "hr", "manager"] }
    notes: text { writeRoles: ["admin"] }
  }
}
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `readRoles` | All roles | Roles allowed to read this field. Fields are stripped from responses for other roles. |
| `writeRoles` | All roles | Roles allowed to write this field. Fields are silently stripped from create/update input for other roles. |

**Read filtering:** When a user with role `"employee"` fetches `/api/employees`, the `salary` and `department` fields are removed from the response. An `"admin"` or `"hr"` user sees all fields.

**Write filtering:** When a user with role `"employee"` POSTs to `/api/employees` with `{ "name": "Carol", "salary": 99999 }`, the `salary` field is silently stripped before the record is created. Only `"admin"` and `"hr"` users can set `salary`.

Unauthenticated requests (no user) have all role-restricted fields stripped on read, and all role-restricted fields stripped on write.

## API Versioning

Version your API by setting `core.api.version`. The version is auto-prefixed into all route paths:

```swift
config {
  core: {
    api: {
      prefix: "/api"
      version: "1"
    }
  }
}
```

Routes are now served at `/api/v1/posts`, `/api/v1/users`, etc. The OpenAPI spec and SDK are also versioned automatically.

### Deprecation

When you bump to a new version, mark old versions as deprecated:

```swift
config {
  core: {
    api: {
      prefix: "/api"
      version: "2"
      deprecatedVersions: ["1"]
      sunsetDate: "Wed, 30 Sep 2026 00:00:00 GMT"
    }
  }
}
```

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `version` | Current API version (auto-prefixed as `/v{version}`) |
| `deprecatedVersions` | Versions that should send deprecation headers |
| `sunsetDate` | HTTP date string for the `Sunset` header |

When the current version is in `deprecatedVersions`, every response includes:
- `Deprecation: true` — signals clients to migrate
- `Sunset: <date>` — when the version will be removed (if `sunsetDate` is set)

## OpenTelemetry & Prometheus

Cequre's monitoring system includes built-in exporters for OpenTelemetry and Prometheus.

### Prometheus Metrics

The Prometheus endpoint is available at `/api/monitor/metrics/prometheus` when monitoring is enabled:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $MONITORING_API_KEY" \
  https://your-app/api/monitor/metrics/prometheus
```

Returns standard Prometheus text format with counters for events, requests, errors, and average duration. Scrape this endpoint with your Prometheus server:

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "cequre"
    metrics_path: "/api/monitor/metrics/prometheus"
    bearer_token: "your-monitoring-api-key"
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["your-app:3000"]
```

### OpenTelemetry Exporter

Send monitoring events to any OTLP-compatible backend (Jaeger, Grafana, Datadog, Honeycomb) via the built-in `OpenTelemetryExporter`:

```typescript
import { OpenTelemetryExporter } from "cequre-ts";

// After runtime.start(), add the exporter:
runtime.monitoring?.addExporter(new OpenTelemetryExporter({
  endpoint: "http://localhost:4318/v1/logs",
  serviceName: "my-cequre-app",
  headers: {}, // optional auth headers
}));
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `endpoint` | Required | OTLP Logs HTTP endpoint (e.g. `http://localhost:4318/v1/logs`) |
| `serviceName` | `"cequre"` | Service name reported to OTLP |
| `headers` | `{}` | Custom headers (e.g. Authorization) |
| `batchSize` | `100` | Events per batch |
| `flushIntervalMs` | `5000` | Flush interval |

The exporter converts Cequre monitoring events to OTLP log records with attributes for HTTP method, path, status code, duration, collection, action, and user ID. Request IDs are mapped to OTLP trace IDs.

# ==========================================
# File: core/vite-plugin.mdx
# ==========================================

# Vite Integration Plugin

The `@cequrebackends/plugin-vite` plugin seamlessly bridges your Cequre backend and Vite frontend into a single dev server running on the same port.

## Automated 1-Step Setup

In any existing Vite project (React, Vue, Svelte, or Vanilla), run:

```bash
cequre add vite
```

This automatically:
1. Installs `@cequrebackends/plugin-vite` in your `package.json`
2. Injects `cequreVite({ autoBuild: true })` into your `vite.config.ts`
3. Initializes your `cequre/schema/config.cequre` DSL directory

---

## Manual Installation

```bash
bun add @cequrebackends/plugin-vite
```

## Usage Examples

### 1. Basic Setup (Zero Config)

For standard project layouts (`cequre/index.ts`, `cequre/routes.ts`, or `api/index.ts`), zero configuration is required:

```typescript
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { cequreVite } from "@cequrebackends/plugin-vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react(),
    cequreVite()
  ]
});
```

Run your regular Vite dev command to start both frontend and backend on the same port:
```bash
bun run dev
```

---

### 2. Full-Stack Production Build Setup (`autoBuild: true`)

Enable `autoBuild: true` so that running `vite build` automatically bundles your Cequre backend alongside your frontend assets:

```typescript
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { cequreVite } from "@cequrebackends/plugin-vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react(),
    cequreVite({
      autoBuild: true // Automatically compiles backend into dist/index.js on `vite build`
    })
  ]
});
```

Run a single command to build both frontend and backend:
```bash
bun run build
```

#### Running the Production Backend Bundle

Once `vite build` completes, run the standalone backend server bundle:

```bash
# Direct execution using Bun
bun dist/index.js

# Or via package.json scripts
bun start
# or
bun run start:api
```

#### Production Container Deployment (`server.Dockerfile`)

When scaffolding a Vite project or running `cequre add vite`, a `server.Dockerfile` is automatically generated in your project root:

```dockerfile
FROM oven/bun:1-alpine AS base
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json bun.lock* ./
RUN bun install

COPY . .
RUN bun run build

FROM oven/bun:1-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app

ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV PORT=3000
ENV HOST=0.0.0.0

COPY --from=base /app/dist /app/dist
COPY --from=base /app/package.json ./

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["bun", "dist/index.js"]
```

To build and launch the production backend container:

```bash
docker build -f server.Dockerfile -t my-cequre-server .
docker run -p 3000:3000 my-cequre-server
```

---

### 3. Custom Entry & API Prefix Auto-Detection

The plugin automatically detects the API prefix directly from your `.cequre` DSL (`prefix: "/v1"` in `config.cequre` or `schema.json`).

If you wish to override the DSL prefix or specify a custom server entry point:

```typescript
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { cequreVite } from "@cequrebackends/plugin-vite";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react(),
    cequreVite({
      entry: "cequre/index.ts",   // Custom server entry point
      apiPrefix: "/v1/api",         // Override proxy prefix (HTTP & WebSockets)
      autoBuild: true,
    })
  ]
});
```

---

### 4. Consuming Generated SDK Client in Frontend

Cequre generates a zero-dependency Client SDK (`cequre-sdk.ts`) alongside your backend. Import `createCequreClient` to interact with your collections using strongly-typed `.get()`, `.post()`, `.patch()`, and `.delete()` methods:

```typescript
// src/App.tsx
import { createCequreClient } from "./cequre-sdk";

// Initialize client (defaults to relative fetches via Vite's dev server port)
const api = createCequreClient();

export default function App() {
  async function handleFetch() {
    const { data: posts, error } = await api.posts.get();
    if (error) {
      console.error("Failed to fetch posts:", error);
      return;
    }
    console.log("Posts:", posts);
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>My App</h1>
      <button onClick={handleFetch}>Load Posts</button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

---

### 5. Programmatic Standalone Build Script

If you prefer building your server outside `vite build`, use the `cequreVite.build()` helper programmatically:

```typescript
// scripts/build-server.ts
import { cequreVite } from "@cequrebackends/plugin-vite";

await cequreVite.build({
  entry: "cequre/index.ts",
  outDir: "build/server",
  outFile: "server.js",
  minify: true,
});
```

---

## Automatic WebSocket, SSE & OpenAPI Support

### Single-Port OpenAPI Documentation (`/api/docs`)
Vite's proxy automatically passes `X-Forwarded-Host` (`req.headers.host`) and `X-Forwarded-Proto` to the backend. When accessing `http://localhost:5173/api/docs`, the OpenAPI specification and Scalar/Swagger UI automatically reflect your single Vite host (`Server: http://localhost:5173`) rather than an internal backend port.

### Realtime SDK Subscriptions (`subscribeWS` & `subscribeSSE`)

The generated SDK client exposes strongly-typed `.subscribeWS()` and `.subscribeSSE()` methods on every collection for listening to realtime CRUD events (`created`, `updated`, `deleted`):

```typescript
import { createCequreClient } from "./cequre/generated/client";

const api = createCequreClient({ baseUrl: "/" });

// 1. Subscribe to WebSocket CRUD events on 'todos' collection
const unsubscribeWS = await api.todos.subscribeWS((event) => {
  console.log("WS Event:", event.type); // 'created' | 'updated' | 'deleted'
  console.log("Data:", event.data);
});

// 2. Subscribe to SSE events on 'todos' collection
const unsubscribeSSE = await api.todos.subscribeSSE((event) => {
  console.log("SSE Event:", event.type, event.data);
});

// 3. Subscribe to custom WebSocket endpoint paths
const unsubscribeCustom = await api.subscribeWS("/api/ws", (data) => {
  console.log("Custom WS payload:", data);
});

// Call returned unsubscribe function when component unmounts
// unsubscribeWS();
```

---

## Options Reference

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `apiPrefix` | `string` | *Auto-detected from `.cequre` DSL* | URL prefix proxied to Cequre backend. Auto-detected from `prefix` in `config.cequre` or defaults to `"/api"`. |
| `entry` | `string` | *Auto-detected* | Custom entry point (`cequre/index.ts`, or legacy `src/server/index.ts`). |
| `autoBuild` | `boolean` | `false` | Automatically bundles Cequre backend during `vite build` (`closeBundle` hook). |

---

## Key Features

- **Single-Port Parity**: Proxies both HTTP requests and WebSocket connections automatically over Vite's dev server port.
- **OpenAPI Host Parity**: Injects `X-Forwarded-Host` so OpenAPI interactive docs (`/api/docs`) display Vite's single host (`http://localhost:5173`).
- **DSL API Prefix Detection**: Automatically syncs proxy prefix with `prefix: "..."` defined in your `config.cequre` DSL.
- **Clean Terminal Output**: Suppresses internal 3001 startup logs so Vite's single URL is the only host shown.
- **Zero Config**: Automatically finds your backend server entry point (`cequre/index.ts`) and probes local binaries without extra setup.
- **SDK Watcher & HMR Trigger**: Automatically watches generated client SDKs (`client.ts`, `sdk.ts`) and triggers Vite HMR reloads on schema updates.
- **Unified Production Build**: Set `autoBuild: true` to compile both your frontend assets and backend server binary during a single `vite build` command.


# ==========================================
# File: ts/access.mdx
# ==========================================

# Access Control

Access control lets you define who can read, create, update, or delete records in each collection. Rules are written in TypeScript in `cequre/routes.ts` (or a module of your own) and evaluated per-request.

## Defining Rules

Access rules can be defined in two places:
1. **Declaratively in the `.cequre` DSL**: Great for fast, simple rules, keeping your schema cohesive.
2. **Programmatically in TypeScript**: Ideal for complex async rules, Row-Level Security, or overriding DSL configurations.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Code overrides DSL.** Any rule defined in your runtime code via `routesModule.access()` will completely override the rule defined in your `.cequre` file for that specific operation. This allows you to define simple baseline rules in the schema, and override specific operations (like `read` or `update`) in your code if they require complex logic.

### 1. Declarative Rules (.cequre DSL)

You can add an `access` block directly inside your collection definition. These rules are compiled natively and evaluated at runtime.

```cequre
collection users {
  auth: true;

  access: {
    // 1. Shorthand boolean (always allow or deny)
    read: true;
    create: true;

    // 2. Expressions using context variables
    update: user.id == id || user.role == "admin";

    // 3. You can also use curly braces for nested or future configurations
    delete: {
      user.role == "admin";
    }
  }

  fields: {
    name: text;
    email: email @unique;
    role: select("admin", "user") @default("user");
  }
}
```

**Available DSL Context Variables:**
- `user`: The currently authenticated user object (e.g. `user.id`, `user.role`).
- `id`: The ID of the document being accessed.
- `data`: The incoming payload for create/update operations.

### 2. Programmatic Rules (TypeScript)

Use `routesModule.access(collectionSlug, rules)` (or `routesModule.access(...)` on the runtime) to register access rules programmatically:

```typescript
// cequre/routes.ts
import { CequreModule } from "cequre-ts";
import type { Collections } from "./_generated/server";

export const routesModule = new CequreModule<Collections>();

routesModule.access("todos", {
  read: (ctx) => true,
  create: (ctx) => ctx.user !== null,
  update: (ctx) => ctx.user?.id === ctx.data.author || ctx.user?.role === "admin",
  delete: (ctx) => ctx.user?.role === "admin",
});
```

Each rule is a function that receives a `CequreRequestContext` and returns `boolean | WhereClause | Promise<boolean | WhereClause>`. 

- If the function returns `true`, the operation is allowed.
- If the function returns `false`, the request is rejected with a `403 Forbidden` error.
- If the function returns a query object (a `WhereClause`), the operation is allowed but the database query is automatically scoped to only match rows satisfying that filter (Row-Level Security).

## Rule Properties

| Rule | When it runs | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| `read` | Before `GET /api/<slug>` and `GET /api/<slug>/:id` | List and single-record queries |
| `create` | Before `POST /api/<slug>` | Create operations |
| `update` | Before `PATCH /api/<slug>/:id` | Update operations |
| `delete` | Before `DELETE /api/<slug>/:id` | Delete operations |

### Auth Rule Properties
For collections with authentication enabled, additional rules govern auth operations:

| Rule | When it runs | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| `register` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/register` | Auth Registration |
| `login` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/login` | Auth Login |
| `refresh` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/refresh` | Auth Refresh Token |
| `logout` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/logout` | Auth Logout |
| `forgotPassword` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/forgot-password` | Auth Forgot Password |
| `resetPassword` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/reset-password` | Auth Reset Password |
| `mfaLogin` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/mfa/login` | MFA Login Step |
| `mfaEnroll` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/mfa/enroll` | MFA Setup |
| `mfaVerify` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/mfa/verify` | MFA Verification |
| `mfaDisable` | Before `POST /api/<slug>/mfa/disable` | MFA Disabling |

## The Context Object

Every rule function receives a `CequreRequestContext`:

```typescript
interface CequreRequestContext {
  request: Request;       // The raw HTTP request
  user: AuthUser | null;  // The authenticated user (or null)
  cequre: CequreRuntime; // The runtime instance
  state?: unknown;        // Optional state from plugins
}

interface AuthUser {
  id: string;
  role: string;
  [key: string]: any;     // All other fields from the user record
}
```

### Using `ctx.user`

The `user` object is populated from the JWT access token (when JWT auth is enabled). It contains all fields from the user's database record except `password`.

```typescript
routesModule.access("posts", {
  // Returns boolean for global access, or a WhereClause for row-level security
  read: (ctx) => {
    if (ctx.user?.role === "admin") return true;
    if (!ctx.user) return false;
    // Regular users can only read their own posts
    return { author: { eq: ctx.user.id } };
  },
  create: (ctx) => ctx.user !== null,
  update: (ctx) => {
    // Only the author or an admin can update
    return ctx.user?.id === ctx.data.author || ctx.user?.role === "admin";
  },
});
```

### Async Rules

Rules can be async — useful for checking external permissions or querying the database:

```typescript
routesModule.access("documents", {
  read: async (ctx) => {
    if (!ctx.user) return false;
    // Check if the user belongs to the organisation that owns the document
    const membership = await ctx.cequre.find("memberships", {
      where: {
        userId: { eq: ctx.user.id },
        orgId: { eq: ctx.data.orgId }
      },
      limit: 1
    });
    return membership.docs.length > 0;
  },
});
```

## Default Behaviour

If an action's access rule is not defined (via `routesModule.access` or the DSL), the default behaviour depends on the type of operation:

- **CRUD Operations (`read`, `create`, `update`, `delete`)**: Default to **DENY**. If you do not specify a rule, the request is rejected with a `403 Forbidden` error.
- **Auth Operations (`login`, `forgotPassword`, `resetPassword`, etc.)**: Default to **ALLOW**. This ensures standard authentication flows continue working without explicit configuration.
- **`register`**: Default to **DENY**. Accounts are managed by the platform (e.g. the admin UI's Settings), so self-registration is never implicitly public. The only implicit exception is the empty-collection bootstrap on the `adminUi` collection — while no admins exist, registration is allowed so the first admin can be created. Afterwards (and for every other auth collection), you must explicitly allow registration:

```typescript
routesModule.access("users", {
  register: () => true // Enable public signup
});
```

Or in the DSL:

```cequre
collection users {
  auth: true;
  access {
    register: true;
  }
}
```

## Multiple Collections

You can register rules for as many collections as needed:

```typescript
routesModule.access("users", {
  read: (ctx) => true,
  create: (ctx) => ctx.user?.role === "admin",
  update: (ctx) => ctx.user?.id === ctx.data.id || ctx.user?.role === "admin",
  delete: (ctx) => ctx.user?.role === "admin",
});

routesModule.access("todos", {
  read: () => true,
  create: () => true,
  update: (ctx) => ctx.user?.id === ctx.data.author,
  delete: (ctx) => ctx.user?.id === ctx.data.author,
});
```

## Globals

Globals support the same `routesModule.access()` API. Use the global's slug as the collection name:

```typescript
routesModule.access("siteSettings", {
  read: () => true,
  update: (ctx) => ctx.user?.role === "admin",
});
```

## Related

- [Hooks](./hooks) — Lifecycle hooks that run before/after CRUD operations
- [Local API](./local-api) — Querying data programmatically inside access rules

# ==========================================
# File: ts/bulk-operations.mdx
# ==========================================

---
title: Bulk Operations
description: Create and delete many documents in a single request with createMany and deleteMany.
---

# Bulk Operations

Bulk operations let you create or delete **many documents in a single request**,
with the same security pipeline (access control, validation, hooks, encryption,
realtime) that single-item CRUD runs — but the database write itself is batched
into one call, so it's dramatically faster than looping single requests.

## When to use them

- Seeding data (imports, migrations, test fixtures)
- Bulk cleanup (delete all expired records)
- Any client that needs to write many rows at once

## Endpoints

```
POST   /api/:slug/bulk     → createMany
DELETE /api/:slug/bulk     → deleteMany
```

### Bulk create

```json
// POST /api/todos/bulk
{
  "items": [
    { "title": "A", "completed": false },
    { "title": "B", "completed": true }
  ]
}
```

```json
// 201 Created
{
  "created": [
    { "id": "01H...", "title": "A", "completed": false },
    { "id": "01H...", "title": "B", "completed": true }
  ],
  "errors": []
}
```

### Bulk delete

```json
// DELETE /api/todos/bulk
{
  "ids": ["01H...", "01H...", "01H..."]
}
```

```json
// 200 OK
{
  "deleted": ["01H...", "01H..."],
  "errors": [
    { "id": "01H...", "error": { "code": "NOT_FOUND", "message": "Not found" } }
  ]
}
```

## Partial failure semantics

Bulk operations are **not all-or-nothing**. Each item runs the pipeline
individually; items that pass are written, items that fail are reported in the
`errors` array with their `index` (create) or `id` (delete). Callers can retry
only the failed subset.

```json
{
  "created": [
    { "id": "01H...", "title": "Good" },
    { "id": "01H...", "title": "Also Good" }
  ],
  "errors": [
    { "index": 1, "error": { "code": "VALIDATION", "message": "title is required" } }
  ]
}
```

## Limits

- **Max batch size: 500 items** per request. Larger batches return `400`.
- Empty `items: []` returns `201` with `created: []` (no-op, not an error).

## SDK usage

The generated client exposes typed methods on every collection:

```ts
// Bulk create
const { data, error } = await api.todos.createMany([
  { title: "A", completed: false },
  { title: "B", completed: true },
]);

// Bulk delete
const { data, error } = await api.todos.deleteMany([
  "01H...", "01H...",
]);
```

## How the pipeline works

Each item goes through the full single-item pipeline **individually**:

1. **Access control** — `checkAccess` per item (row-level rules apply)
2. **Field stripping** — `stripForbiddenFields` + `filterWritableFields` per item
3. **Validation** — `validateCreate` per item
4. **Before hooks** — `beforeCreate` / `beforeDelete` per item
5. **Batched DB write** — `adapter.createMany` / `adapter.deleteMany` (one call)
6. **After hooks** — `afterCreate` / `afterDelete` per item
7. **Realtime** — one `created` / `deleted` event per item
8. **Cache invalidation** — once for the whole batch

Field encryption (`@encrypt`) is applied per item before the batched write and
decrypted on the response, exactly like single-item creates.

## File cleanup on bulk delete

If the collection has `upload` / `media` / `file` fields, bulk delete fetches
each record before deleting and enqueues physical file deletions — identical
to the single-item DELETE behavior.


# ==========================================
# File: ts/client-sdk.mdx
# ==========================================

# Zero-Dependency Client SDK

Cequre automatically generates a **zero-dependency Client SDK** (`cequre-sdk.ts`) alongside your backend every time you compile. This standalone, perfectly-synced TypeScript file provides end-to-end type safety, real-time subscriptions, and native fetch bindings without requiring any external NPM packages.

Because the entire SDK logic and types exist in a single file, LLMs and AI Agents can read it directly without guessing your API surface. You can pass the SDK to an agent and say "build me a dashboard for my data"—it will instantly write flawless, fully-typed integrations against your Cequre backend on the first try.

## Usage & Client Configuration

Initialize the client using `createCequreClient`:

```typescript
import { createCequreClient } from './cequre-sdk';

export const api = createCequreClient({
  baseUrl: "http://localhost:3000",
  // Auto-inject your auth bearer token into every request
  getToken: () => localStorage.getItem("token"),
  // Pass credentials for cookie-based authentication ("include" | "same-origin" | "omit")
  credentials: "include",
  // Global response interceptor
  onResponse: (res) => {
    if (res.status === 401) {
      console.warn("Session expired");
    }
  }
});
```

### Configuration Options Reference

| Property | Type | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `baseUrl` | `string` | Base server URL (defaults to relative `""` in Vite dev server). |
| `getToken` | `() => string \| null \| Promise<string \| null>` | Dynamic callback to resolve the bearer token for `Authorization` headers. |
| `token` | `string` | Static bearer token. |
| `credentials` | `"include" \| "same-origin" \| "omit"` | Fetch credentials mode for sending cookies. |
| `onResponse` | `(response: SDKResponse<any>) => void` | Global response interceptor hook called after every request. |

---

### Basic CRUD

The SDK automatically mirrors your collections and exposes strongly-typed `.get()`, `.post()`, `.patch()`, `.delete()`, `.createMany()`, and `.deleteMany()` methods:

```typescript
// Create a user
const { data: newUser, error } = await api.users.post({ 
  name: "Alice", 
  email: "alice@example.com" 
});

// List users with filtering
const { data: activeUsers } = await api.users.get({
  query: {
    where: { status: "active" },
    limit: 10
  }
});

// Update a user
await api.users.patch(newUser.id, { status: "inactive" });

// Delete a user
await api.users.delete(newUser.id);

// Bulk create — one batched DB write
const { data: bulkCreated } = await api.users.createMany([
  { name: "Bob", email: "bob@example.com" },
  { name: "Carol", email: "carol@example.com" },
]);

// Bulk delete
await api.users.deleteMany([bulkCreated.created[0].id, bulkCreated.created[1].id]);
```

Bulk methods return `{ created, errors }` / `{ deleted, errors }` — partial
failures are reported per item. See [Bulk Operations](/ts/bulk-operations) for
the full contract.

---

### Authentication

If a collection is configured with `auth: true` (e.g. `users`), the SDK automatically centralizes its authentication endpoints under the `.auth` namespace.

```typescript
// Register a new user
const { data: regRes, error: regErr } = await api.auth.register({ 
  email: "alice@example.com", 
  password: "securePassword123!" 
});

// Login
const { data: session } = await api.auth.login({ 
  email: "alice@example.com", 
  password: "securePassword123!" 
});

// The SDK can automatically use session.accessToken if you configured getToken()
console.log("Logged in with token:", session.accessToken);
```

---

### File Uploads (Multipart Form Data)

The SDK natively understands `File` and `Blob` objects. If you pass a `File` in your payload, the SDK engine seamlessly converts the entire request into a `multipart/form-data` payload under the hood. You never have to manually construct `FormData`.

```typescript
const fileInput = document.getElementById("avatar") as HTMLInputElement;
const file = fileInput.files![0];

await api.users.patch(userId, {
  name: "Alice",
  avatar: file // Handled automatically!
});
```

---

### Realtime Subscriptions

If you have enabled Realtime, the SDK provides cleanly-typed methods for both WebSockets and Server-Sent Events (SSE).

```typescript
// Listen for real-time changes using WebSockets
const unsubscribe = api.users.subscribeWS((event) => {
  console.log("User updated!", event.data);
});

// Or using Server-Sent Events (SSE)
const unsubscribeSSE = api.users.subscribeSSE((event) => {
  console.log("User updated via SSE!", event.data);
});
```

---

## Reactive Realtime Client (`createCequreRealtimeClient`)

While `createCequreClient` provides a stateless, imperative HTTP client, `createCequreRealtimeClient` provides a **Convex-style reactive query and mutation engine**.

It maintains an in-memory observable query cache, automatically reconciles incremental changes (`created`, `updated`, `deleted`) from multiplexed WebSockets / Server-Sent Events, and provides instant optimistic UI updates with zero boilerplate.

### Realtime Client Setup

```typescript
import { createCequreRealtimeClient } from './cequre-sdk';

export const liveApi = createCequreRealtimeClient({
  baseUrl: "http://localhost:3000",
  getToken: () => localStorage.getItem("token"),
  // Primary transport: "ws" (default) or "sse"
  transport: "ws",
  // Replay missed events upon reconnection via Durable Streams (default: true)
  autoCatchUp: true,
});
```

### 1. One-Shot Typed Queries

Returns collection documents directly as a typed array:

```typescript
// Fetches active todos directly as Todos[]
const activeTodos = await liveApi.todos.query({
  query: {
    where: { completed: false },
    sort: { createdAt: "desc" },
    limit: 20
  }
});
```

### 2. Live Reactive Subscriptions

Subscribes to live state. The callback is invoked initially with current cached data, and automatically called with the **fresh updated array** whenever any matching record is created, modified, or deleted:

```typescript
const unsubscribe = liveApi.todos.subscribe(
  { query: { where: { completed: false } } },
  (liveTodos) => {
    // liveTodos is always the complete, fresh Todos[] array!
    console.log("Current active todos:", liveTodos);
  }
);

// Unsubscribe when done / component unmounts
unsubscribe();
```

### 3. Optimistic Mutations

Mutations immediately insert, update, or remove the document in all matching local query subscriptions in 0ms, then commit the change to the server in the background (with automatic rollback on error):

```typescript
// 1. Optimistic Create
const newTodo = await liveApi.todos.mutate.create({
  title: "Write documentation",
  completed: false,
});

// 2. Optimistic Patch
await liveApi.todos.mutate.patch(newTodo.id, {
  completed: true,
});

// 3. Optimistic Delete
await liveApi.todos.mutate.delete(newTodo.id);
```

### 4. UI Framework Integration

Because `createCequreRealtimeClient` is framework-agnostic, integrating with your favorite frontend library takes only a few lines of code:

#### React (using native `useSyncExternalStore`)

```typescript
import { useSyncExternalStore } from "react";
import { liveApi } from "./api";

export function useLiveTodos(queryInput?: any) {
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    (onStoreChange) => liveApi.todos.subscribe(queryInput, onStoreChange),
    () => liveApi.todos.query(queryInput)
  );
}
```

#### Vue 3 (`ref` + `onUnmounted`)

```typescript
import { ref, onUnmounted } from "vue";
import { liveApi } from "./api";

export function useLiveTodos(queryInput?: any) {
  const todos = ref([]);
  const unsub = liveApi.todos.subscribe(queryInput, (data) => {
    todos.value = data;
  });
  onUnmounted(unsub);
  return todos;
}
```

#### Svelte 5 (`readable` store)

```typescript
import { readable } from "svelte/store";
import { liveApi } from "./api";

export function liveTodosStore(queryInput?: any) {
  return readable([], (set) => {
    return liveApi.todos.subscribe(queryInput, set);
  });
}
```

---

### Custom Streams (HTTP Readable Streams)

If you have created a custom endpoint on your Cequre backend and marked it with `{ stream: true }`, the SDK generator will automatically generate a streaming method. These methods return an `AsyncGenerator` that you can seamlessly consume using `for await`.

```typescript
// Call a custom streaming endpoint
const stream = await api.myCustomRoute.get();

// Consume the stream as chunks arrive
for await (const chunk of stream) {
  console.log("Received chunk:", chunk);
}
```

---

### Custom Endpoints with Query Parameters

When you define a custom route with a `query` schema, the generated SDK automatically produces a typed method that accepts query parameters. The SDK serializes them via `URLSearchParams` and appends them to the request URL.

**Backend route:**

```typescript
// cequre/routes.ts
routesModule.get(
  "/api/firm-controls",
  async ({ query }) => {
    const { page = 1, limit = 10, status = "" } = query || {};
    return { echoPage: Number(page), echoLimit: Number(limit), echoStatus: status };
  },
  {
    response: t.Object({
      echoPage: t.Number(),
      echoLimit: t.Number(),
      echoStatus: t.String(),
    }),
    query: t.Object({
      page: t.Optional(t.Number()),
      limit: t.Optional(t.Number()),
      status: t.Optional(t.String()),
    }),
  }
);
```

**SDK usage:**

```typescript
// Query params are typed from the route's `query` schema
const { data } = await api.firmControls.get({
  query: { page: 2, limit: 20, status: "Active" },
});

// Request URL: /api/firm-controls?page=2&limit=20&status=Active
console.log(data); // { echoPage: 2, echoLimit: 20, echoStatus: "Active" }
```

For POST/PUT/PATCH routes with a `query` schema, the SDK accepts both `data` (request body) and `params.query`:

```typescript
await api.searchResults.post({
  data: { keywords: "cequre" },
  params: { query: { page: 1, limit: 10 } },
});
```

---

## Server-Side Usage (SSR / Loaders)

If you are using a framework like Remix, Next.js App Router, or Nuxt, you will often need to execute queries on the server on behalf of a specific user.

To prevent token leakage across requests, the SDK provides the `.withToken(token)` method. This creates an isolated, shallow clone of the client strictly bound to that user's token.

```typescript
// In your Remix Loader or Next.js Server Component
export async function loader({ request }: { request: Request }) {
  const token = getCookieToken(request);
  
  // Safe isolated clone for this specific HTTP request
  const serverApi = api.withToken(token);
  
  const { data: myData } = await serverApi.posts.get();
  return Response.json(myData);
}
```

---

## AI Agent Integration (MCP)

If you are using the **Cequre Builder API** or the **Cequre MCP Server**, the system automatically returns the absolute URL to your generated SDK after a successful build or deploy. 

Agents can read the usage instructions baked directly into the SDK header and start scripting against your API immediately.


# ==========================================
# File: ts/custom-endpoints.mdx
# ==========================================

# Custom Endpoints

The auto-generated CRUD routes cover most data operations, but you often need custom endpoints — webhooks, aggregations, health checks, or integration with external services. The runtime lets you add arbitrary HTTP routes alongside the generated ones.

> [!TIP]
> Custom routes can live on the exported app (registered directly) or inside a `CequreModule`. See [App Patterns](../core/app-patterns) for when to use each.

## Adding Routes

Add custom routes on the `routesModule` in `cequre/routes.ts` (the scaffolded custom-routes module). Use `.get()`, `.post()`, `.put()`, `.patch()`, or `.delete()`:

```typescript
// cequre/routes.ts
import { CequreModule, t } from "cequre-ts";
import type { Collections } from "./_generated/server";

export const routesModule = new CequreModule<Collections>();

// Simple GET route
routesModule.get("/greeting", () => {
  return { greeting: "hello from cequre" };
});

// Route with path params
routesModule.get("/users/:id/profile", (ctx) => {
  return { userId: ctx.params.id };
});
```

The route methods accept two overloads — `(path, handler, options)` or `(path, options, handler)` — and the handler is fully typed against your `Collections` schema.

## The Route Context

Each handler receives a `CequreRouteContext`:

```typescript
interface CequreRouteContext {
  request: Request;        // The raw HTTP request
  url: URL;                // Parsed URL (lazy)
  params: Record<string, string>; // Path params (e.g. :id)
  query: Record<string, string | string[]>; // Query string params
  body: unknown;           // Parsed body (when body schema is defined)
  user: AuthUser | null;   // Authenticated user
  cequre: CequreRuntime; // Runtime instance
  state?: unknown;         // Plugin state
}
```

### Typed `ctx.user` with `@saveToJWT`

`ctx.user` is typed against your auth collection: the generated `Collections` registry carries a `__auth` marker that resolves `ctx.user` to the auth collection's document shape **plus** `role`. That means any field you mark `@saveToJWT` on the auth collection is directly accessible (and autocompleted) on `ctx.user` in custom routes, hooks, and access rules:

```cequre
collection users {
  auth: true;
  fields {
    email: email @unique;
    nickname: text @saveToJWT @optional;      // scalar → embedded in JWT
    workspaceId: link("workspaces")[] @on("user") @saveToJWT; // link → target id embedded
  }
}
```

```typescript
// cequre/routes.ts
routesModule.get("/api/custom/profile", (ctx) => {
  if (!ctx.user) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });
  const nickname = ctx.user.nickname;       // string | undefined — typed
  const workspaceId = ctx.user.workspaceId; // Array<string> | undefined — typed
  return new Response(JSON.stringify({ nickname, workspaceId });
});
```

These fields are populated from the JWT payload at request time (no DB lookup) — scalar `@saveToJWT` fields embed their value directly, and `link(...)` fields embed the linked record's id.

The same typed `ctx.user` applies everywhere the request context appears:

- **Collection hooks** (`app.hooks("users", { beforeCreate: ({ user }) => ... })`) — `user` is the auth collection + `role`
- **Access rules** (`app.access("users", { read: ({ user }) => ... })`) — same
- **Plugin hooks** (`beforeRequest` / `afterRequest` / `onError`) — when the plugin is declared through the typed config (`createCequre({ plugins: [...] }))`), `ctx.user` resolves to the auth user too

In all of these, `@saveToJWT` fields are typed and autocompleted, and fields that don't exist on the auth collection are compile errors.

### What `ctx.user` does *not* carry

`ctx.user` is built from the **JWT payload** — so it only contains `id`, `role`, and whatever you marked `@saveToJWT`. Hidden fields (`@hidden`, e.g. the injected `_verified` / `_verificationToken` / MFA fields) are **not** JWT claims and are **not** on `ctx.user` — reading them there is a compile error:

```typescript
// ❌ _verified is hidden + omit — never in the JWT, not on ctx.user
const isVerified = ctx.user?._verified;   // TS error: Property '_verified' does not exist

// ✅ check it server-side with a DB lookup (includeHidden is server-only)
const user = await ctx.cequre.findById("users", ctx.user.id, { includeHidden: true });
if (!user?._verified) throw CequreError.Forbidden("Your account hasn't been verified");
```

A bare `CequrePlugin` (no type argument) gets the strict `AuthUser` fallback (`id` only) — unknown fields squiggle instead of silently passing as `any`. Declare plugins through the typed config (`createCequre({ plugins: [...] }))`) to get the full auth-collection shape with `@saveToJWT` fields.

### Typed plugins

Import `CequrePlugin` from the generated `server.ts`:

```typescript
import type { CequrePlugin } from "./cequre/_generated/server";

export const validatorPlugin: CequrePlugin = {
  name: "validator",
  beforeRequest: (ctx) => {
    const u = ctx.user;
    if (u) {
      void u.nickname;      // ✅ any Users field
      void u.workspaceId;   // ✅ any Users field
      // u._verify           // ❌ TS error — not on Users
    }
  },
};
```

`ctx.user` is the full auth collection type — every field, not just `@saveToJWT`. The same alias exists for `CequreRequestContext` (custom route handlers), and `beforeHandle` guards on route options receive the same typed user.

## Path Parameters

Use `:param` syntax in the path. Parameters are available in `ctx.params`:

```typescript
routesModule.get("/users/:id", (ctx) => {
  return { id: ctx.params.id };
});

routesModule.get("/posts/:slug/comments/:commentId", (ctx) => {
  return {
    slug: ctx.params.slug,
    commentId: ctx.params.commentId,
  };
});
```

## Query Parameters

Query string parameters are available in `ctx.query`:

```typescript
routesModule.get("/search", (ctx) => {
  const q = ctx.query.q as string;
  const page = parseInt(ctx.query.page as string) || 1;
  return { query: q, page };
});
```

## Schema Validation

Use [TypeBox](https://github.com/sinclairzx/typebox) (exported as `t` from the runtime) to validate request bodies, query params, and responses. Invalid inputs are rejected with a `400` error before your handler runs:

```typescript
routesModule.post(
  "/users/:id/transfer",
  (ctx) => {
    // ctx.body is typed and validated
    const { amount, toUserId } = ctx.body;
    // ctx.params.id is typed and validated
    return { transferred: amount, from: ctx.params.id, to: toUserId };
  },
  {
    body: t.Object({
      amount: t.Number({ minimum: 1 }),
      toUserId: t.String(),
    }),
    params: t.Object({
      id: t.String(),
    }),
    response: t.Object({
      transferred: t.Number(),
      from: t.String(),
      to: t.String(),
    }),
  }
);
```

### Schema Options

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `body` | TypeBox schema for the request body (JSON). Validates POST/PUT/PATCH bodies. |
| `query` | TypeBox schema for query string parameters. Also generates typed query params in the Client SDK. |
| `params` | TypeBox schema for path parameters. |
| `response` | TypeBox schema for the response body. |
| `detail` | OpenAPI metadata: `{ summary, description, tags }`. |
| `authRequired` | When `true`, rejects unauthenticated requests with `401`. |

> [!TIP]
> When you define a `query` schema, the generated Client SDK automatically produces a method that accepts typed query parameters. See [Client SDK - Custom Endpoints with Query Parameters](./client-sdk#custom-endpoints-with-query-parameters) for details.

## Returning Responses

Handlers can return plain objects (auto-converted to JSON), `Response` objects, or throw errors:

```typescript
// Return a plain object (200 OK, application/json)
routesModule.get("/stats", () => {
  return { totalUsers: 42, activeSessions: 7 };
});

// Return a Response directly
routesModule.get("/html", () => {
  return new Response("<h1>Hello</h1>", {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "text/html" },
  });
});

// Return with custom status
routesModule.post("/webhooks/stripe", (ctx) => {
  // Process webhook...
  return new Response(JSON.stringify({ received: true }), {
    status: 202,
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  });
});
```

## Using the Runtime Inside Routes

Access the database and other runtime features via `ctx.cequre`:

```typescript
routesModule.get("/dashboard/:userId", async (ctx) => {
  const userId = ctx.params.userId;

  const [todos, posts] = await Promise.all([
    ctx.cequre.find("todos", { where: { author: { eq: userId } }, limit: 10 }),
    ctx.cequre.find("posts", { where: { author: { eq: userId } }, limit: 5 }),
  ]);

  return {
    todos: todos.docs,
    posts: posts.docs,
    totalTodos: todos.totalDocs,
    totalPosts: posts.totalDocs,
  };
});
```

## Auth-Required Routes

Set `authRequired: true` to reject unauthenticated requests:

```typescript
routesModule.get(
  "/admin/stats",
  (ctx) => {
    return { users: ctx.cequre.count("users") };
  },
  { authRequired: true }
);
```

## Zero-JS Static Responses

For routes that serve the exact same bytes on every request — favicons, icons,
hashed assets, a cached HTML shell — pass `nativeResponse`. The response is
built once at startup and registered directly in Bun's native route map, so
serving it runs no framework code at all (no plugin dispatch, no per-request
allocation):

```typescript
const FAVICON = new Response(FAVICON_SVG, {
  headers: { "Content-Type": "image/svg+xml", "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" },
});

routesModule.get("/favicon.svg", () => FAVICON, { nativeResponse: FAVICON });
```

Because the response bypasses all middleware, only use this for content that is
truly immutable and needs no auth, CORS reflection, or security headers.
Eligibility rules enforced by the router: static paths only (no `:params`),
method-specific routes only (not `all()`), and skipped automatically when CORS
is configured.

## OpenAPI Documentation

Routes with `detail` and schema options are included in the auto-generated OpenAPI spec at `/api/docs`:

```typescript
routesModule.get(
  "/health",
  () => ({ status: "ok", uptime: process.uptime() }),
  {
    response: t.Object({ status: t.String(), uptime: t.Number() }),
    detail: {
      summary: "Health check",
      description: "Returns server health status",
      tags: ["system"],
    },
  }
);
```

## Related

- [Local API](./local-api) — Querying data programmatically
- [Access Control](./access) — How access rules interact with custom routes
- [REST API](./rest-api) — The auto-generated CRUD endpoints

# ==========================================
# File: ts/database-plugins.mdx
# ==========================================

# Database Adapters

Cequre supports five database engines. Each implements the `CequreAdapter` interface and ships directly from `cequre-ts` — no separate packages to install. You pick the one that matches your `DATABASE_URL`.

## Quick Reference

| Database | URL Scheme | Class | Package to install (driver) |
|---|---|---|---|
| SQLite | `file:` or `sqlite:` | `SQLiteAdapter` | None (uses `bun:sqlite`) |
| PostgreSQL | `postgres:` or `postgresql:` | `PostgresAdapter` | `postgres` |
| SurrealDB | `http:` or `https:` | `SurrealDBAdapter` | `surrealdb` |
| Turso | `libsql:` or `file:` | `TursoAdapter` | `@libsql/client` |
| MongoDB | `mongodb:` or `mongodb+srv:` | `MongoDBAdapter` | `mongodb` |

All adapter classes and factory functions are exported from `cequre-ts`:

