# Resend Plugin

The Resend plugin lets Cequre send lifecycle emails (password resets, email verifications, welcome emails) via the Resend REST API, bypassing legacy SMTP for faster and more reliable delivery. It's installed via the CLI scaffold, which drops a `CequreEmailTransport` implementation into your project.

## Installation

```bash
cequre plugin add resend
```

This creates `cequre/plugins/resend/index.ts` and appends the required env var to `.env`:

```env
RESEND_API_KEY=re_your_api_key_here
```

## Configuration

The scaffold exports `resendTransport` — a `CequreEmailTransport` implementation. Provide it to the email configuration:

```typescript
import { createCequre } from "../_generated/server";
import { SQLiteAdapter } from "cequre-ts";
import { resendTransport } from "../plugins/resend";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new SQLiteAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
  email: {
    from: "onboarding@resend.dev",
    appName: "My Awesome SaaS",
    transport: resendTransport,
  },
});
```

## Features

- **Fast Delivery:** Uses Resend's modern REST API instead of slower SMTP connections.
- **Beautiful Built-ins:** Seamlessly integrates with Cequre's default email templates for forgot password and verification workflows.

# File: ts/plugins/rpc.mdx
# ==========================================

# RPC Client SDK Plugin

Cequre provides a fully-typed frontend RPC client plugin to consume your API in React, Vite, or any browser application. It dynamically infers your backend schema types to provide complete end-to-end type safety.

## Installation

```bash
bun add @cequrebackends/plugin-rpc
```

## Usage Example

Import the client and initialize it using your auto-generated `Collections` type from your backend.

```typescript
import { createRpc } from "@cequrebackends/plugin-rpc";
// Import your generated types from the Cequre backend (this ensures end-to-end type safety)
import type { Collections } from "../backend/src/cequre"; 

// 1. Initialize the client
const token = localStorage.getItem("token");

export const api = createRpc<Collections>("http://localhost:3000/api", {
  headers: token ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } : {},
  credentials: "include", // Important if you're using cookie-based auth
  onResponse: (response) => {
    // Global interceptor logic
    if (response.status === 401) {
      window.location.href = "/login";
    }
  }
});

// 2. Fetching Data (Read)
async function fetchActiveTodos() {
  const result = await api.todos.find({ 
    query: { status: "active" } 
  });
  console.log(`Found ${result.total} active todos!`, result.docs);
}

// 3. Simple Create (JSON)
async function createTodo() {
  const newTodo = await api.todos.create({ 
    title: "Finish the RPC plugin", 
    completed: false 
  });
  console.log("Created ID:", newTodo.id);
}

// 4. File Upload via Form Data Auto-Detection
async function updateUserAvatar(fileInput: HTMLInputElement) {
  const photoFile = fileInput.files?.[0];
  if (!photoFile) return;

  // Because 'photoFile' is a File object, the client automatically switches 
  // from application/json to multipart/form-data for this request!
  const updatedUser = await api.users.update("user_123", { 
    name: "John", 
    avatar: photoFile 
  });
}

// 5. Explicit Global Upload
async function uploadRawFile(file: File) {
  const { url, filename } = await api.upload(file);
  console.log("File uploaded to:", url);
}

// 6. Real-time Streams (SSE)
function listenForUpdates() {
  const sse = api.todos.sse();

  sse.onmessage = (event) => {
    const update = JSON.parse(event.data);
    console.log("A todo was updated on the server:", update);
  };
}

// 7. WebSockets
function connectToChat() {
  const ws = api.messages.ws({ query: { room: "general" } });
  
  ws.onopen = () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "hello" }));
  ws.onmessage = (msg) => console.log("Incoming WebSocket Message:", msg.data);
}
```


# ==========================================
# File: ts/plugins/s3.mdx
# ==========================================

# S3 Storage Plugin

The S3 storage plugin routes Cequre's file uploads directly to AWS S3 (or any S3-compatible API like Cloudflare R2, MinIO, or DigitalOcean Spaces). It's installed via the CLI scaffold, which drops a `StorageProvider` implementation into your project.

## Installation

```bash
cequre plugin add s3
```

This creates `cequre/plugins/s3/index.ts` (using `aws4fetch`) and appends the required env vars to `.env`:

```env
S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=your_access_key
S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=your_secret_access_key
S3_BUCKET=my-bucket
S3_REGION=us-east-1
S3_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:9000
```

## Configuration

The scaffold exports `s3StorageProvider` — a `StorageProvider` implementation. Wire it in:

```typescript
import { createCequre } from "./_generated/server";
import { sqlite } from "cequre-ts";
import { s3StorageProvider } from "./plugins/s3";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: sqlite({ url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! }),
  storage: s3StorageProvider,
});

app.start({ port: Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000 });
```

## Features

- **Zero-Config Overrides:** Once registered, any `.cequre` schema collection field that uses the `upload` type, or any raw API calls to `/upload`, will seamlessly save files to S3 instead of local disk.
- **Proxy Serving:** Uploaded files are served back through `/api/uploads/:filename` — the runtime calls the provider's `getFile()` to stream content from S3, so your frontend never needs to know the S3 endpoint.
- **S3-Compatible:** Works with AWS S3, MinIO, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean Spaces, and any S3-compatible API (set `S3_ENDPOINT` for path-style services).

# SQLite Adapter

Cequre's SQLite database adapter ships directly in the embedded runtime (`cequre-ts`) — no separate package to install. It runs on Bun's incredibly fast native SQLite driver (`bun:sqlite`).

## Usage

```typescript
import { createCequre } from "../_generated/server";
import { SQLiteAdapter } from "cequre-ts";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new SQLiteAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
});
```

Or use the `sqlite()` factory:

```typescript
import { createCequre } from "../_generated/server";
import { sqlite } from "cequre-ts";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: sqlite({ url: process.env.DATABASE_URL || "sqlite.db" }),
});
```

## Features

- **Blazing Fast:** Uses `bun:sqlite` under the hood. No heavy native node modules or compilation steps needed.
- **Auto-Migrations:** Works seamlessly with `cequre db:sync`.
- **JSON support:** Safely stores arrays and objects in JSON text fields while maintaining Cequre's schema guarantees.

# SurrealDB Adapter

import { createCequre } from "../_generated/server";

export const app = createCequre({

    url: process.env.SURREAL_URL!, // e.g. http://localhost:8000
    namespace: "cequre",

import { createCequre } from "../_generated/server";

export const app = createCequre({

  }),

# ==========================================
# File: ts/queue-manager.mdx
# ==========================================

# Queue Manager

Cequre includes a `CequreQueueManager` built on [BullMQ](https://docs.bullmq.io/) for background job processing. Use it for email sending, data processing, scheduled tasks, or any work that should run outside the request-response cycle.

The manager is a thin singleton that handles Redis connection config, shutdown ordering, and cron integration. `getQueue()` and `registerWorker()` return raw BullMQ `Queue` and `Worker` objects, so you get the full BullMQ API without any wrapper.

## Setup

The queue manager requires a Redis connection. Initialise it once at startup:

```typescript
import { CequreQueueManager } from "cequre-ts";

// Initialise once — creates the singleton
CequreQueueManager.initialize({
  bullmq: {
    connection: {
      host: process.env.REDIS_HOST || "localhost",
      port: parseInt(process.env.REDIS_PORT || "6379"),
    },
  },
});
```

## Adding Jobs

Push jobs to a queue by name:

```typescript
const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();

// Add a single job
const job = await qm.addJob("emails", "send-welcome", {
  to: "user@example.com",
  name: "John",
});

// Add with options
const job = await qm.addJob("reports", "generate-monthly", {
  userId: "abc-123",
  month: "2026-06",
}, {
  attempts: 3,
  backoff: { type: "exponential", delay: 5000 },
  removeOnComplete: true,
});

// Add bulk jobs
await qm.addBulk("notifications", [
  { name: "notify", data: { userId: "user-1", message: "Hello" } },
  { name: "notify", data: { userId: "user-2", message: "Hello" } },
  { name: "notify", data: { userId: "user-3", message: "Hello" } },
]);
```

## Registering Workers

Workers process jobs from a queue. Register a handler for each queue:

> `registerWorker` is async and resolves once the worker is connected to Redis. Always `await` it before enqueuing jobs to avoid a race condition where jobs are added before the worker can process them.

```typescript
const worker = await qm.registerWorker("emails", async (job) => {
  console.log(`Processing ${job.name}:`, job.data);

  if (job.name === "send-welcome") {
    await sendWelcomeEmail(job.data.to, job.data.name);
  }
});

const reportWorker = await qm.registerWorker("reports", async (job) => {
  if (job.name === "generate-monthly") {
    const report = await generateReport(job.data.userId, job.data.month);
    await saveReport(report);
  }
});
```

`registerWorker` returns the raw BullMQ `Worker` instance. See the [BullMQ Worker docs](https://api.docs.bullmq.io/classes/v5.Worker.html) for the full API.

## Integration with Cron

When the queue manager is initialised, cron jobs automatically use BullMQ's repeatable jobs instead of local `Bun.cron`:

```typescript
import { app } from "./index";

// If CequreQueueManager is initialised, this creates a BullMQ repeatable job
// If not, it falls back to Bun.cron (local, single-process)
app.cron("daily-report", "0 9 * * *", async (app) => {
  const users = await app.find("users", { limit: 1000 });
  for (const user of users.docs) {
    await CequreQueueManager.getInstance().addJob("reports", "daily-summary", {
      userId: user.id,
    });
  }
});
```

## Job Options

BullMQ job options supported via the `opts` parameter:

| Option | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `attempts` | `number` | Number of retry attempts on failure |
| `backoff` | `{ type: "exponential" \| "fixed", delay: number }` | Retry backoff strategy |
| `delay` | `number` | Delay before processing (ms) |
| `removeOnComplete` | `boolean \| number` | Remove on completion |
| `removeOnFail` | `boolean \| number` | Remove on failure |
| `repeat` | `{ pattern: string }` | Cron pattern for repeatable jobs |
| `priority` | `number` | Higher priority = processed first |
| `jobId` | `string` | Custom job ID for deduplication (see Idempotent Jobs) |

## Managing Repeatable Jobs

```typescript
const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();
const queue = qm.getQueue("cequre_cron");

// List repeatable jobs
const repeatable = await queue.getRepeatableJobs();

// Remove a repeatable job by key
await queue.removeRepeatableByKey(repeatable[0].key);
```

## Health Checks

Check Redis connectivity and queue depth using BullMQ's native API:

```typescript
const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();
const queue = qm.getQueue("emails");

// Check Redis is reachable
const client = await queue.client;
await client.ping(); // "PONG"

// Get queue depth by state
const counts = await queue.getJobCounts("waiting", "active", "delayed", "failed");
// { waiting: 3, active: 1, delayed: 0, failed: 2 }

// Check all registered queues
for (const [name, queue] of qm.getQueueMap()) {
  const counts = await queue.getJobCounts("waiting", "active", "failed");
  console.log(`${name}:`, counts);
}
```

For a custom health endpoint:

```typescript
app.router.get("/health/queues", async (ctx) => {
  const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();
  const queue = qm.getQueue("emails");
  const client = await queue.client;

  try {
    await client.ping();
    const counts = await queue.getJobCounts("waiting", "active", "failed");
    return Response.json({ redis: true, ...counts });
  } catch {
    return Response.json({ redis: false }, { status: 503 });
  }
});
```

## Failed Jobs

BullMQ keeps failed jobs in the queue's failed set. Inspect and retry them without any extra configuration:

```typescript
const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();
const queue = qm.getQueue("emails");

// Get failed jobs
const failed = await queue.getFailed();

// Inspect a failed job
console.log(failed[0].id, failed[0].data, failed[0].failedReason);

// Retry a failed job
await failed[0].retry();

// Remove a failed job
await failed[0].remove();
```

## Idempotent Jobs

Prevent duplicate jobs by passing a unique `jobId`. If a job with that ID already exists, BullMQ skips the duplicate:

```typescript
const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();

// First call enqueues the job
await qm.addJob("reports", "monthly", { userId: "123" }, { jobId: "user-123-monthly" });

// Second call with the same jobId is a no-op
await qm.addJob("reports", "monthly", { userId: "123" }, { jobId: "user-123-monthly" });
```

Use this when a webhook may fire twice, or when a user may double-click a button.

## Rate Limiting

Limit job throughput per queue using BullMQ's `rateLimit` option:

```typescript
const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();

// Global rate limit via defaultWorkerOptions
CequreQueueManager.initialize({
  bullmq: { connection: { host: "localhost", port: 6379 } },
  defaultWorkerOptions: {
    rateLimit: { max: 10, duration: 1000 }, // 10 jobs per second
  },
});

// Or per-worker rate limit
await qm.registerWorker("emails", handler, {
  rateLimit: { max: 5, duration: 1000 }, // 5 emails per second
});
```

## Metrics and Events

`registerWorker` returns a raw BullMQ `Worker`. Listen to its events for metrics, logging, or monitoring:

```typescript
const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();

const worker = await qm.registerWorker("emails", async (job) => {
  await sendEmail(job.data.to);
});

// Job lifecycle events
worker.on("completed", (job) => {
  console.log(`[metrics] completed: ${job.queueName}/${job.id}`);
});

worker.on("failed", (job, err) => {
  console.error(`[metrics] failed: ${job?.queueName}/${job?.id} — ${err.message}`);
});

// Worker-level events
worker.on("error", (err) => {
  console.error(`[metrics] worker error: ${err.message}`);
});

// Check worker status
console.log(worker.isRunning()); // true when actively processing
```

See the [BullMQ Worker docs](https://api.docs.bullmq.io/classes/v5.Worker.html) for the full event list.

## Graceful Shutdown

The queue manager cleans up workers, queues, and event listeners on shutdown:

```typescript
const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();
await qm.close();
// Closes all workers, queue event listeners, and queue connections
```

When you call `server.stop()`, Cequre automatically stops all cron jobs. For queue cleanup, call `qm.close()` before stopping the server.

## Full Example

```typescript
// src/queue.ts
import { CequreQueueManager } from "cequre-ts";
import { app } from "./index";

// 1. Initialise with Redis
CequreQueueManager.initialize({
  bullmq: {
    connection: {
      host: process.env.REDIS_HOST!,
      port: 6379,
    },
  },
});

const qm = CequreQueueManager.getInstance();

// 2. Register workers
await qm.registerWorker("emails", async (job) => {
  if (job.name === "send-welcome") {
    await app.mailer?.sendWelcome(job.data.to);
  }
});

await qm.registerWorker("notifications", async (job) => {
  if (job.name === "notify") {
    await sendPushNotification(job.data.userId, job.data.message);
  }
});

// 3. Enqueue from hooks
app.hooks("users", {
  afterCreate: async ({ data }) => {
    await qm.addJob("emails", "send-welcome", { to: data.email });
  },
});
```

## Related

- [Hooks](./hooks) — Enqueue jobs from lifecycle hooks
- [Realtime](./realtime) — Pushing changes to connected clients

# ==========================================
# File: ts/rest-api.mdx
# ==========================================

# REST API

Every collection in your Cequre schema automatically gets a full set of REST endpoints. These endpoints handle CRUD operations, filtering, sorting, pagination, and authentication — no code required.

## Base URL

All API endpoints are mounted under the API prefix defined in your `config.cequre`:

```cequre
config {
  core: {
    api: {
      prefix: "/api"
    }
  }
}
```

If your prefix is `/api` and you have a collection called `todos`, the endpoints are at `/api/todos`.

## Collection Endpoints

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/<prefix>/<slug>` | List records (with filtering, sorting, pagination) |
| `GET` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/:id` | Get a single record by ID |
| `POST` | `/<prefix>/<slug>` | Create a new record |
| `PATCH` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/:id` | Update a record |
| `DELETE` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/:id` | Delete a record |

## Authentication Endpoints

When a collection has `auth: true`, additional endpoints are generated:

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/register` | Register a new user |
| `POST` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/login` | Login with email/password |
| `POST` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/refresh` | Refresh an access token |
| `POST` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/logout` | Logout (revokes refresh token) |
| `POST` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/forgot-password` | Request a password reset email |
| `POST` | `/<prefix>/<slug>/reset-password` | Reset password with a token |

## Global Endpoints

Globals get two endpoints — one for reading, one for updating the singleton document:

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/<prefix>/globals/<slug>` | Get the global document |
| `POST` / `PATCH` | `/<prefix>/globals/<slug>` | Create or update the global document |

## System Endpoints

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/<prefix>/docs` | Interactive API docs (Scalar) |
| `GET` | `/<prefix>/docs/openapi.json` | OpenAPI specification |
| `POST` | `/<prefix>/upload` | Upload a file |
| `GET` | `/<prefix>/uploads/:filename` | Serve an uploaded file |
| `GET` | `/<prefix>/ws` | WebSocket connection (if realtime is enabled) |
| `GET` | `/<prefix>/sse` | Server-Sent Events (if realtime is enabled) |

## Querying

### Filter

Use `where` query parameter with JSON to filter records:

```bash
# Filter by exact match
GET /api/todos?where={"completed":{"eq":false}}

# Filter by multiple fields
GET /api/todos?where={"completed":{"eq":false},"priority":{"eq":"high"}}

# Using OR
GET /api/todos?where={"OR":[{"completed":{"eq":false}},{"priority":{"eq":"urgent"}}]}
```

### Filter Operators

| Operator | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `eq` | Equals | `{"title":{"eq":"Buy milk"}}` |
| `neq` | Not equals | `{"completed":{"neq":true}}` |
| `gt` | Greater than | `{"price":{"gt":100}}` |
| `gte` | Greater than or equal | `{"price":{"gte":100}}` |
| `lt` | Less than | `{"price":{"lt":50}}` |
| `lte` | Less than or equal | `{"price":{"lte":50}}` |
| `in` | In array | `{"status":{"in":["draft","published"]}}` |
| `nin` | Not in array | `{"status":{"nin":["archived"]}}` |
| `like` | LIKE pattern | `{"title":{"like":"%grocer%"}}` |
| `nlike` | NOT LIKE | `{"title":{"nlike":"%test%"}}` |

### Sort

Prefix with `-` for descending:

```bash
GET /api/todos?sort=-createdAt        # newest first
GET /api/todos?sort=priority           # ascending
GET /api/todos?sort=-priority,createdAt # multiple fields
```

### Pagination

```bash
GET /api/todos?limit=10&page=1
```

### Populate Relationships

Use `depth` to populate relationship fields:

```bash
# depth=0 (default): author is just the ID
GET /api/todos?depth=0

# depth=1: author is the full user object
GET /api/todos?depth=1
```

## Response Format

### List Response

```json
{
  "docs": [
    { "id": "abc-123", "title": "Buy groceries", "completed": false, ... },
    { "id": "def-456", "title": "Walk the dog", "completed": true, ... }
  ],
  "totalDocs": 42,
  "limit": 10,
  "page": 1,
  "totalPages": 5,
  "hasNextPage": true,
  "hasPrevPage": false
}
```

### Single Record

```json
{
  "id": "abc-123",
  "title": "Buy groceries",
  "completed": false,
  "author": "user-uuid",
  "createdAt": "2026-07-01T12:00:00.000Z",
  "updatedAt": "2026-07-01T12:00:00.000Z"
}
```

### Create Response

Status `201 Created` — returns the created record.

### Delete Response

```json
{ "deleted": true }
```

## Authentication

When JWT auth is enabled, include the access token in the `Authorization` header:

```bash
# Authenticated request
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>" http://localhost:3000/api/todos
```

### Register

```bash
POST /api/users/register
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "user@example.com",
  "password": "securepassword",
  "name": "John Doe"
}
```

Response:

```json
{
  "user": { "id": "abc-123", "email": "user@example.com", "name": "John Doe" },
  "accessToken": "eyJ...",
  "refreshToken": "eyJ...",
  "message": "Registration successful"
}
```

### Login

```bash
POST /api/users/login
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "user@example.com",
  "password": "securepassword"
}
```

### Refresh Token

```bash
POST /api/users/refresh
Content-Type: application/json

{ "refreshToken": "eyJ..." }
```

### Forgot Password

```bash
POST /api/users/forgot-password
Content-Type: application/json

{ "email": "user@example.com" }
```

Always returns `200` with a generic message to prevent email enumeration.

### Reset Password

```bash
POST /api/users/reset-password
Content-Type: application/json

{ "token": "reset-token-from-email", "password": "newpassword" }
```

## Caching

When a collection has `cache` configured, `GET` responses include an `X-Cache` header:

- `X-Cache: HIT` — served from cache
- `X-Cache: MISS` — fetched from database (and cached for subsequent requests)

Cache is automatically invalidated on create, update, or delete operations for that collection.

## Rate Limiting

When rate limiting is configured in `security.rateLimit`, requests exceeding the limit receive a `429 Too Many Requests` response.

## OpenAPI Documentation

Every Cequre server includes auto-generated API documentation at `/<prefix>/docs` (powered by Scalar). The OpenAPI JSON spec is available at `/<prefix>/docs/openapi.json`.

Custom routes with schema definitions and `detail` metadata are included in the spec.

## Related

- [Local API](./local-api) — Programmatic data access from TypeScript
- [Access Control](./access) — How access rules affect REST endpoints
- [Custom Endpoints](./custom-endpoints) — Adding routes beyond the CRUD API

# ==========================================
# File: ts/scaffolded-plugins.mdx
# ==========================================

# Scaffolded Plugins

Cequre ships with a set of ready-to-use plugin scaffolds. Running `cequre plugin add <name>` drops a fully typed TypeScript file into `cequre/plugins/<name>/index.ts`, updates the barrel file at `cequre/plugins/index.ts`, and appends the required environment variables to your `.env`.

**Plugins are just scripts.** The scaffolded file is a plain TypeScript module that implements a Cequre interface and exports an object. There is no hidden framework magic — you own the file, you read it, you edit it. This is intentional: you should never be debugging inside `node_modules` to understand what your storage or email provider does.

## Available Plugins

| Plugin | Category | Command | Package |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S3 Storage** | Storage | `cequre plugin add s3` | `aws4fetch` |
| **Resend** | Email | `cequre plugin add resend` | `resend` |
| **Nodemailer** | Email | `cequre plugin add nodemailer` | `nodemailer` |
| **Durable Streams** | Streams | `cequre plugin add durable-streams` | `ioredis` |

## What Happens When You Run `cequre plugin add`

1. Creates `cequre/plugins/<name>/index.ts` with the full template
2. Updates `cequre/plugins/index.ts` barrel file with `export * from "./<name>"`
3. Appends required env vars to `.env` (or `.env.local`) with a comment header
4. Installs the npm package(s) via your detected package manager

You then import the scaffolded export in your `app.ts` and wire it into `createCequre()`.

## S3 Storage

S3-compatible storage using `aws4fetch`. Works with AWS S3, MinIO, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean Spaces, and any S3-compatible API.

```bash
cequre plugin add s3
```

```env
S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=your_access_key
S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=your_secret_key
S3_BUCKET=my-bucket
S3_REGION=us-east-1
S3_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:9000
```

The scaffold exports `s3StorageProvider` — a `StorageProvider` implementation. Wire it in:

```typescript
import { s3StorageProvider } from "../plugins/s3";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new SQLiteAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
  storage: s3StorageProvider,
});
```

Files are uploaded directly to S3 via `aws4fetch` and served back through the `/api/uploads/:filename` proxy — the runtime calls `getFile()` on the provider to stream content from S3. The `url` field in `UploadedFile` always points to `/api/uploads/:filename`, so your frontend never needs to know the S3 endpoint.

For MinIO or other S3-compatible services, set `S3_ENDPOINT` to your service URL. The scaffold automatically handles path-style vs virtual-host-style URLs based on whether the endpoint ends with the bucket name.

## Resend

Transactional email via the [Resend](https://resend.com) REST API.

```bash
cequre plugin add resend
```

```env
RESEND_API_KEY=re_your_api_key_here
```

The scaffold exports `resendTransport` — a `CequreEmailTransport` implementation. Wire it in:

```typescript
import { resendTransport } from "../plugins/resend";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new SQLiteAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
  email: {
    from: '"My App" <no-reply@myapp.com>',
    transport: resendTransport,
  },
});
```

## Nodemailer

SMTP email via the industry-standard `nodemailer` library. Works with SendGrid, Mailgun, AWS SES, and any SMTP server.

```bash
cequre plugin add nodemailer
```

```env
SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USER=user@example.com
SMTP_PASS=secret
SMTP_FROM="App" <no-reply@example.com>
SMTP_SECURE=false
```

The scaffold exports `nodemailerTransport`. Wire it in:

```typescript
import { nodemailerTransport } from "../plugins/nodemailer";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new SQLiteAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
  email: {
    from: process.env.SMTP_FROM!,
    transport: nodemailerTransport,
  },
});
```

## Durable Streams

Redis-backed durable stream store for resumable SSE streams.

```bash
cequre plugin add durable-streams
```

```env
REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379
```

The scaffold exports `durableStreamStore` — a `DurableStreamStore` implementation. Wire it in:

```typescript
import { durableStreamStore } from "../plugins/durable-streams";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new SQLiteAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
  durableStreams: durableStreamStore,
});
```

## The Barrel File

Every scaffolded plugin is re-exported from `cequre/plugins/index.ts`:

```typescript
export * from "./s3";
export * from "./resend";
export * from "./nodemailer";
export * from "./durable-streams";
```

This lets you import from a single path if you prefer:

```typescript
import { s3StorageProvider, resendTransport } from "../plugins";
```

## Related

- [Plugins](./plugins) — the plugin interface and writing custom plugins
- [Storage](./storage) — the `StorageProvider` interface and upload proxy
- [Email](./email) — Email transport configuration
- [CLI Reference](./cli-reference) — `cequre plugin add` and `cequre adapter add`


# ==========================================
# File: ts/sse.mdx
# ==========================================

# Server-Sent Events (SSE)

SSE provides unidirectional server-to-client push over HTTP. Simpler than WebSocket — no custom protocol, works through proxies.

## Enabling SSE

In your `.cequre` file, you can enable SSE for a collection. The runtime will automatically broadcast CRUD events to connected clients.

```cequre
collection todos {
  realtime: {
    sse: ["create", "update", "delete"] // true = all events
  }
  fields: {
    title: text
  }
}
```

When enabled, the runtime mounts `GET /api/sse` as the Server-Sent Events endpoint.

## Connecting

```javascript
const es = new EventSource("http://localhost:3000/api/sse?channel=todos");

es.onmessage = (event) => {
  const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log(data);
};
```

On connect, the server sends:

```
event: connected
data: {"id":"conn-uuid","channels":["todos"],"authenticated":false}
```

## Subscribing to Channels

Pass channel names via query parameters:

```bash
# Single channel
GET /api/sse?channel=todos

# Multiple channels
GET /api/sse?channel=todos&channel=posts

# Or comma-separated
GET /api/sse?channels=todos,posts
```

## Receiving Change Events

When a CRUD operation occurs on a collection you've subscribed to, you receive an event containing the action data:

```
data: {"event":"todos:created","data":{"id":"abc-123","title":"Buy groceries"}}
```

## SSE Manager API

You can programmatically broadcast SSE from anywhere in your TypeScript code:

```typescript
import { CequreSSE } from "cequre-ts";

// Broadcast to a channel
CequreSSE.broadcastToChannel("todos", {
  event: "todos:created",
  data: { id: "abc-123", title: "New todo" }
});

// Broadcast to all connections
CequreSSE.broadcastAll({ type: "announcement", data: "Hello everyone" });

// Send to a specific connection
CequreSSE.sendTo(connectionId, { event: "custom", data: "private message" });

// Stats
const stats = CequreSSE.getStats();
// { connections: 8, channels: { todos: 5, posts: 3 } }
```


# ==========================================
# File: ts/storage.mdx
# ==========================================

# File Storage

Cequre provides a pluggable storage system for handling file uploads. The default `LocalStorageProvider` saves files to disk. For production, scaffold the S3 plugin to store files in cloud storage.

## How Uploads Work

When a collection has an `upload` field, the runtime auto-generates a global upload endpoint:

```
POST /api/upload          → Upload a file
GET  /api/uploads/:filename → Serve an uploaded file
```

The upload endpoint accepts `multipart/form-data` with a `file` field and returns metadata about the stored file.

## Uploading a File

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/upload \
  -F "file=@photo.jpg"
```

Response:

```json
{
  "filename": "01J5A8X2K3M4N5P6Q7R8S9T0VW.jpg",
  "originalName": "photo.jpg",
  "mimetype": "image/jpeg",
  "size": 2048576,
  "url": "/api/uploads/01J5A8X2K3M4N5P6Q7R8S9T0VW.jpg"
}
```

## Default: Local Storage

By default, Cequre uses `LocalStorageProvider` which saves files to an `uploads/` directory on disk:

```typescript
// This is the default — no configuration needed
export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: sqlite({ url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! }),
});
```

Files are served at `/api/uploads/:filename`. The upload directory is created automatically.

## Image Transforms

Uploaded raster images (JPEG, PNG, WebP) can be transformed on the fly by appending query parameters to the serve URL. Derivatives are cached on disk (in `uploads/.derivatives/`) and served with immutable cache headers, so repeated requests are fast and CDN-friendly.

```
GET /api/uploads/photo.jpg?w=800&h=600&fit=inside&fmt=webp&q=80
```

| Param | Values | Default | Notes |
|-------|--------|---------|-------|
| `w`, `h` | 1–4096 | — | At least one required to trigger a resize |
| `fit` | `fill` \| `inside` | `fill` with w+h, else `inside` | `inside` preserves aspect ratio and fits within the box; `fill` stretches to exact dimensions. Upscaling never happens (`withoutEnlargement` is always on). |
| `fmt` | `webp` \| `jpeg` \| `png` | source format | `fmt` alone (no `w`/`h`) converts format only |
| `q` | 1–100 | 80 | jpeg/webp quality |

Examples:

```bash
# 320px-wide thumbnail as WebP
curl -o thumb.webp "http://localhost:3000/api/uploads/photo.jpg?w=320&fmt=webp"

# Fit within a 800x600 box, keep source format
curl -o box.jpg "http://localhost:3000/api/uploads/photo.jpg?w=800&h=600&fit=inside"
```

With the generated client SDK:

```typescript
const thumb = await client.uploads.get("photo.jpg", { w: 320, fmt: "webp" });
```

Notes:

- Requests without transform params serve the original file unchanged.
- Invalid parameters return `400`. Non-image files ignore transform params and pass through.
- Transform requests against non-raster extensions (e.g. `.svg`, `.pdf`) or S3-backed storage serve the original file.
- AVIF output is intentionally not supported (the platform encoder is unavailable on Linux).

## S3 Storage

For production, scaffold the S3 plugin to store files in AWS S3, MinIO, DigitalOcean Spaces, Cloudflare R2, or any S3-compatible service.

```bash
cequre plugin add s3
```

This creates `cequre/plugins/s3/index.ts` with a `StorageProvider` implementation using `aws4fetch`, and appends the required env vars to your `.env`:

```env
S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=your_access_key
S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=your_secret_key
S3_BUCKET=my-bucket
S3_REGION=us-east-1
S3_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:9000
```

Wire the scaffolded provider into your app:

```typescript
import { createCequre } from "../_generated/server";
import { SQLiteAdapter } from "cequre-ts";
import { s3StorageProvider } from "../plugins/s3";

export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: new SQLiteAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL!),
  storage: s3StorageProvider,
});
```

### How File Serving Works with S3

When a file is uploaded, the S3 provider stores it directly in the bucket and returns a `url` of `/api/uploads/:filename`. When a client requests that URL, the runtime calls the provider's `getFile()` method to stream the file content back through the Cequre server. Your frontend never needs to know the S3 endpoint or construct direct URLs.

For MinIO or other S3-compatible services, set `S3_ENDPOINT` to your service URL. The scaffold handles path-style vs virtual-host-style URLs based on whether the endpoint already ends with the bucket name.

See [Plugins](./plugins) for more on the `cequre plugin add` workflow.

## The StorageProvider Interface

Both local and S3 storage implement the `StorageProvider` interface:

```typescript
interface StorageProvider {
  /** Save a file and return its metadata */
  saveFile(file: File, options?: { filename?: string }): Promise<UploadedFile>;

  /** Delete a file by its reference filename */
  deleteFile(filename: string): Promise<void>;

  /** Optional: Fetch file content directly for proxying through /api/uploads/:filename.
   *  Return a Response, or an object with data + contentType. */
  getFile?(filename: string): Promise<Response | { data: Uint8Array | ArrayBuffer | ReadableStream; contentType?: string } | undefined>;

  /** Optional: Return a direct or presigned URL for the file */
  getFileUrl?(filename: string): Promise<string | undefined>;

  /** Optional: Multipart upload for massive files */
  initMultipartUpload?(options: { filename: string; mimetype: string; size: number }): Promise<{ uploadId: string; filename: string; parts?: { partNumber: number; url: string }[] }>;
  completeMultipartUpload?(uploadId: string, filename: string, parts: { partNumber: number; etag?: string }[]): Promise<UploadedFile>;
}

interface UploadedFile {
  filename: string;
  originalName: string;
  mimetype: string;
  size: number;
  url: string;
}
```

### File Serving Priority

When a request hits `/api/uploads/:filename`, the runtime checks the storage provider in this order:

1. **`getFile()`** — If implemented, streams file content directly from the provider (e.g. S3 proxy). Returns the `Response` or `{ data, contentType }` object.
2. **`getFileUrl()`** — If implemented, returns a redirect to a direct or presigned URL.
3. **Local disk fallback** — Reads from the local `uploads/` directory (default `LocalStorageProvider` behavior).

## Writing a Custom Storage Provider

Implement `StorageProvider` to use any storage backend — Cloudflare R2, Azure Blob, Google Cloud Storage, etc:

```typescript
import type { StorageProvider, UploadedFile } from "cequre-ts";

class R2StorageProvider implements StorageProvider {
  async saveFile(file: File): Promise<UploadedFile> {
    // Upload to R2
    return { filename: "...", originalName: file.name, mimetype: file.type, size: file.size, url: "/api/uploads/..." };
  }

  async getFile(filename: string) {
    // Stream content back from R2
    const res = await fetch(`https://my-r2-bucket.r2.dev/${filename}`);
    return res;
  }

  async deleteFile(filename: string): Promise<void> {
    // Delete from R2
  }
}

// Register it
export const app = createCequre({
  adapter: sqlite({ url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! }),
  storage: new R2StorageProvider(),
});
```

## Streaming Large File Uploads

For handling massive files (e.g. multi-gigabyte videos or archives) without crashing the browser or running your server out of memory, Cequre provides a built-in streaming upload utility:

```typescript
// From your frontend client
const { data, error } = await api.uploads.uploadLargeFile(myMassiveFile, {
  onProgress: (percent) => console.log(`Upload progress: ${percent}%`)
});

if (data) {
  // Attach the returned metadata directly to an upload field
  await api.videos.create({
    title: "My Vacation",
    video: data
  });
}
```

### The Streaming Architecture
The `api.uploads.uploadLargeFile` utility streams the binary payload directly to `POST /api/uploads/stream` while receiving real-time NDJSON progress events:

1. **Direct-to-Cloud S3 Streaming:** If your storage provider implements multipart uploads (e.g. S3 / RustFS / R2), the server streams 5MB chunks on the fly into presigned multipart parts.
2. **Memory-Safe Local Disk Streaming:** If you are using `LocalStorageProvider` (or local filesystem), the server streams the incoming chunks directly into a temporary file on disk without buffering multi-GB payloads into RAM.

### S3 CORS Requirements
If you are using the S3 plugin for direct-to-cloud uploads, your frontend browser will be making `PUT` requests directly to Amazon S3. You **must** configure your S3 bucket's CORS policy to allow this.

In your AWS S3 Console, add this CORS configuration to your bucket:
```json
[
    {
        "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
        "AllowedMethods": ["PUT", "POST", "GET"],
        "AllowedOrigins": ["https://your-frontend-domain.com", "http://localhost:3000"],
        "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"]
    }
]
```
> [!IMPORTANT]
> The `ExposeHeaders: ["ETag"]` rule is absolutely critical. Without it, the frontend SDK cannot read the `ETag` returned by AWS for each chunk, and the upload will fail to finalize!

## Using Uploads in Collections

Declare an `upload` field in your schema to store file metadata:

```cequre
collection products {
  fields: {
    name: text
    image: upload @optional
    gallery: upload[] @optional
  }
}
```

When you create or update a record, pass the upload response's `filename` or `url` as the field value:

```bash
# 1. Upload the file
curl -X POST /api/upload -F "file=@product.jpg"
# → { "filename": "01J5...", "url": "/api/uploads/01J5...", ... }

# 2. Create the product with the uploaded file URL
curl -X POST /api/products \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Widget", "image": "01J5A8X2K3M4N5P6Q7R8S9T0VW.jpg"}'
```

## Related

- [Plugins](./plugins) — `cequre plugin add s3` and all available scaffolds
- [Collections](./collections) — Defining `upload` fields in the DSL

# ==========================================
# File: ts/utilities.mdx
# ==========================================

# Standalone Utilities (`CequreUtils`)

Cequre bundles a collection of zero-dependency, high-throughput utility tools under the **`CequreUtils`** namespace. 

By grouping all utilities under `CequreUtils`, your project benefits from:
- **Zero Import Collisions**: Eliminates naming conflicts with Node.js built-ins (`crypto`, `url`) or 3rd-party packages (`ulid`, `ms`, `pino`).
- **Single Import Ergonomics**: Import a single object and access all helpers via IDE autocompletion.
- **Zero Dependency Overhead**: All utilities are built natively using standard WebCrypto and modern JavaScript APIs.

---

## Quickstart

```typescript
import { CequreUtils } from "@cequrebackends/cequre";

// 1. Generate a Sortable Unique ID
const orderId = CequreUtils.ulid();

// 2. Parse Human Durations (returns seconds)
const ttlSeconds = CequreUtils.duration("2h"); // 7200

// 3. Cryptographic Hashing
const hash = await CequreUtils.crypto.sha256("my-secret-key");

// 4. Structured Logging
const log = CequreUtils.logger("billing");
log.info({ orderId }, "Payment processed");

// 5. Persistent Key-Value Store
const kv = new CequreUtils.KV({ driver: "sqlite" });
await kv.set("user:123", { name: "Alice" }, 3600);
```

---

## 1. Unique Identifiers (`CequreUtils.ulid`)

Generates 26-character Crockford Base32 lexicographically sortable identifiers (monotonic timestamps + entropy).

```typescript
// Generate a new ULID
const id = CequreUtils.ulid();
// => "01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV"

// Extract creation Date from an existing ULID
const date = CequreUtils.ulidToDate(id);

// Check if a string is a valid ULID
const isValid = CequreUtils.isValidULID(id); // true
```

---

## 2. Duration Parser (`CequreUtils.duration`)

Converts human-readable time strings into numeric seconds.

```typescript
CequreUtils.duration("30s");   // 30
CequreUtils.duration("15m");   // 900
CequreUtils.duration("2h");    // 7200
CequreUtils.duration("7d");    // 604800
```

---

## 3. Cryptography & Security (`CequreUtils.crypto`)

Zero-dependency cryptographic helpers built with WebCrypto.

```typescript
// SHA-256 Hex Digest
const hash = await CequreUtils.crypto.sha256("password123");

// HMAC-SHA256 Signature
const signature = await CequreUtils.crypto.hmac("payload-data", "secret-key");

// Constant-Time String Comparison (Mitigates timing attacks)
const isMatch = CequreUtils.crypto.timingSafeEqual(signature, receivedSignature);

// Secure Random Token
const token = CequreUtils.crypto.randomToken(32); // 64 hex chars
```

---

## 4. Structured Logging (`CequreUtils.logger`)

Returns a high-performance Pino JSON logger instance tagged with the specified component name.

```typescript
const log = CequreUtils.logger("stripe-webhook");

log.info({ event: "charge.succeeded", amount: 4999 }, "Charge captured");
log.error({ err: new Error("Webhook failed") }, "Webhook processing failed");
```

---

## 5. URL Helpers (`CequreUtils.url`)

Ultra-fast URL parsing utilities optimized for hot HTTP request pipelines.

```typescript
// Extract pathname without query string or hash
const pathname = CequreUtils.url.extractPathname("http://localhost:3000/api/users?role=admin");
// => "/api/users"

// Fast query parameter parser
const query = CequreUtils.url.parseQuery("http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=2&limit=25");
// => { page: "2", limit: "25" }
```

---

## 6. AWS S3 & SigV4 Streaming (`CequreUtils.s3`)

Stream files directly from AWS S3, MinIO, or DigitalOcean Spaces with native HTTP 206 Partial Content range request support.

```typescript
const s3Config = {
  bucket: "my-bucket",
  region: "us-east-1",
  accessKeyId: process.env.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID!,
  secretAccessKey: process.env.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY!,
};

// Build canonical S3 URL
const fileUrl = CequreUtils.s3.buildUrl("videos/sample.mp4", s3Config);

// Proxy stream directly to client with range headers
app.router.get("/media/video.mp4", async (ctx) => {
  return CequreUtils.s3.stream(ctx.request, "videos/sample.mp4", s3Config);
});
```

---

## 7. Key-Value Storage (`CequreUtils.KV`)

Multi-backend key-value store facade supporting `memory`, `sqlite`, and `redis`.

```typescript
// SQLite-backed persistent KV
const kv = new CequreUtils.KV({ 
  driver: "sqlite", 
  sqlite: { path: "./data/kv.db" } 
});

// Set with 1-hour TTL (in seconds)
await kv.set("rate_limit:user_1", 1, 3600);

// Get value
const count = await kv.get<number>("rate_limit:user_1");

// Prefix scan
const userKeys = await kv.keys("rate_limit:");
```

---

## 8. Background Queue & Durable Jobs (`CequreUtils.queue` / `durableQueue`)

```typescript
// In-memory concurrent queue worker (backed by Effect fibers)
const queue = CequreUtils.queue.getInstance();
queue.addJob(async () => {
  await sendSlackNotification("New sign up");
});
```


# ==========================================
# File: ts/websockets.mdx
# ==========================================

# WebSockets

WebSocket provides bidirectional, persistent connections with room-based pub/sub. Cequre automatically configures WebSocket endpoints when enabled in your DSL.

## Enabling WebSockets

In your `.cequre` file, you can enable WebSockets for a collection. The runtime will automatically broadcast CRUD events to connected clients.

```cequre
collection todos {
  realtime: {
    ws: ["create", "update", "delete"] // true = all events
  }
  fields: {
    title: text
  }
}
```

When enabled, the runtime mounts `GET /api/ws` as the WebSocket upgrade endpoint.

## Connecting

```javascript
const ws = new WebSocket("ws://localhost:3000/api/ws");

ws.onmessage = (event) => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log(msg);
};
```

On connect, the server sends:

```json
{ "type": "connected", "id": "conn-uuid" }
```

## Joining a Room

Join a collection's room to receive change events:

```javascript
ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "join", room: "todos" }));
```

Response:

```json
{ "type": "joined", "room": "todos" }
```

## Receiving Change Events

When a CRUD operation occurs on a collection you've joined, you receive:

```json
{
  "event": "todos:created",
  "data": { "id": "abc-123", "title": "Buy groceries", "completed": false }
}
```

The event name follows the pattern `<collection>:<action>`:
- `todos:created`
- `todos:updated`
- `todos:deleted`

## Leaving a Room

```javascript
ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "leave", room: "todos" }));
```

## Broadcasting to a Room

From your TypeScript code, broadcast a custom message to all connections in a room:

```typescript
import { CequreWebsocket } from "cequre-ts";

CequreWebsocket.broadcastToRoom("todos", {
  type: "notification",
  message: "System maintenance in 10 minutes",
});
```

## WebSocket Manager API

```typescript
// Send to a specific connection
CequreWebsocket.sendTo(connectionId, { type: "ping" });

// Broadcast to all connections
CequreWebsocket.broadcastAll({ type: "announcement" });

// Broadcast with exclusions
CequreWebsocket.broadcastToRoom("todos", payload, { exclude: [senderId] });

// Get room members
const members = CequreWebsocket.getRoomMembers("todos");

// Stats
const stats = CequreWebsocket.getStats();
// { connections: 15, rooms: { todos: 12, posts: 3 }, heartbeatActive: true }
```

## Ping/Pong Heartbeat

The WebSocket manager has a built-in heartbeat to detect dead connections:

```javascript
// Client responds to server pings
ws.onmessage = (event) => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(event.data);
  if (msg.type === "ping") {
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "pong" }));
  }
};
```
